title: analyze_portfolio positions_text subscripts many holding keys directly; one missing/None field crashes the whole analysis
description: The f-string uses p['symbol'], p['name'], p['asset_type'], p['shares'], p['avg_cost'] (formatted :.2f), p['market_value'] (:,.0f), p['weight_pct'] (:.1f), p['unrealized_pnl'] (:+,.0f), p['unrealized_pct'] (:+.1f), and p['current_price']. Any None among avg_cost/market_value/weight_pct/unrealized_pnl/unrealized_pct raises 'unsupported format string passed to NoneType.__format__', and any missing key raises KeyError — both caught by the outer except (line 844) which then falls back to rule-based, silently discarding the real AI analysis even though most positions were fine.
fix: Build each position line defensively: coerce numerics with (p.get('avg_cost') or 0) etc. and guard current_price (already done). This prevents one malformed holding from forcing the entire portfolio onto the rule-based fallback.

title: Leased API secret persisted on broker instance for object lifetime, defeating short-lived lease TTL
description: _lease_keys() leases the Alpaca key/secret (default ttl_s=300) but immediately copies the plaintext into self._key/self._secret, which live for the entire lifetime of the AlpacaBroker object — long past the 300s lease expiry. The whole point of aj_secrets.Lease is short-lived, scoped material that callers must not persist; storing the raw values on a long-lived instance attribute defeats that guarantee and keeps live-trading credentials resident in memory indefinitely.
fix: Store the Lease objects (self._kid_lease, self._sec_lease) and read .value inside _headers() each request, re-leasing if expired; or lease per-request in _request(). At minimum, re-lease on expiry rather than caching the plaintext string permanently.

title: Kelly avg-win/avg-loss uses t["realized"] which can KeyError
description: _kelly_factor filters wins/losses with float(t.get('realized') or 0) (None-safe) but then computes avg_win/avg_loss with float(t['realized']). realized_trades() always sets 'realized', but the monkeypatchable _realized_trades wrapper and any externally-supplied trade dict (tests, other brokers) may omit it; the get() guard elsewhere shows the author expects it can be absent. A missing key raises KeyError inside the try-less arithmetic block, which is caught by sizing_multiplier's broad except and silently neutralised to 1.0 — defeating Kelly sizing.
fix: Replace sum(float(t['realized']) ...) with sum(float(t.get('realized') or 0) ...) in both avg_win and avg_loss computations to match the None-safe access used two lines above.

title: Sector-cap and per-symbol-weight use marks.get(s) or avg_cost where mark may be 0.0
description: In gate 11 mv = qty * (marks.get(s) or float(p.get('avg_cost') or 0)). aj_risk._marks may legitimately return 0.0 for a symbol with no quote; `0.0 or avg_cost` falls back to avg_cost which is the intended guard, so that's fine. But marks.get(s) returning None for a symbol NOT in the dict is also handled. The real bug: when marks.get(s) is a valid small positive mark, fine — however if every mark is None and every avg_cost is 0 (dust), total stays 0 and the cap silently passes. Low risk but the same `x or y` idiom in aj_rules line 250 masks a genuine 0.0 mark as 'missing', understating book value and letting weight caps be bypassed.
fix: Use an explicit None check: mark = marks.get(s); px = mark if mark is not None else float(p.get('avg_cost') or 0). Apply in aj_alpha gate 11 and aj_rules gate ⑩.

title: TP-ladder rungs scale out fixed fractions of CURRENT qty, over-selling on repeat cycles
description: extra_exit_signals returns round(qty/2,6) for rung-2 and round(qty/3,6) for rung-1 of the CURRENT position qty each cycle. Because the ladder fires every cycle the gain condition holds, it will repeatedly emit qty/3 (or qty/2) of whatever remains, so the position is sold down in a geometric series rather than 'a third' once. The comment says 'scale out a third at tp / 1.5tp / 2tp' — meaning one third of the ORIGINAL position per rung, fired once. As written, once gain >= tp the agent keeps dumping 1/3 of the remaining shares every cycle.
fix: Track which rungs have already fired per symbol (e.g. persist in aj_position_state or a settings key) and only emit each rung once; or size each rung off the original opened qty and gate on a 'rung_fired' flag so repeats are suppressed.

title: Bear-regime nudge RAISES sell_prob_threshold, making the agent sell LESS in a downturn
description: In effective_config bear branch, eff['sell_prob_threshold'] is increased by +0.03 (clamped 0.30-0.50). A higher sell threshold means the model needs MORE conviction to sell, i.e. it sells less readily — the opposite of risk-off behaviour you want in a bear regime. The buy threshold is correctly raised (harder to buy) but the sell threshold change is inverted relative to intent ('regime-adaptive profile' / protect capital in bear).
fix: Lower the sell threshold in bear (e.g. eff['sell_prob_threshold'] = _clamp(base - 0.03, 0.30, 0.50)) so the agent exits more readily, matching the risk-off intent.

title: trade_stats accesses t["realized"] without None-safety, KeyError on malformed trade
description: wins = [t for t in trades if t['realized']>0] and sum(t['realized'] ...) index 'realized' directly. realized_trades() sets it, but trade_stats is called from many places (status, escalation, reflection) and a single malformed row (e.g. from a partial migration) raises KeyError that is NOT caught here — it propagates up into status()/maybe_escalate(). Contrast with aj_alpha which uses t.get('realized') or 0.
fix: Use t.get('realized') or 0 consistently for the comparisons and sums, matching the defensive access used elsewhere.

title: build_reflection worst-name guard can pick best as worst and crash on attrib[-1] semantics
description: worst = attrib[-1] if attrib and attrib[-1].get('total',0) < 0 else None. attribution() is sorted descending by total, so attrib[-1] is the LOWEST total — correct for 'worst'. But best = attrib[0] (highest). If the list has a single element that is negative, best and worst are the SAME row, double-reporting it. More importantly attribution() entries are dicts so .get is safe, but the worst row's total<0 check uses .get('total',0) while best is unconditional — if all totals are >=0, worst is None (fine). The single-element negative case mislabels one name as both best and worst.
fix: Guard worst to a distinct row: worst = attrib[-1] if len(attrib)>1 and attrib[-1].get('total',0)<0 else None (or compare identity to best).

title: PaperBroker limit-order marketability uses spot quote but ignores that buy fills can exceed limit via adverse slippage
description: For a marketable buy (quote<=lp) fill_price = min(lp, quote*(1+adverse)). That's correct. But for sell, fill_price=max(lp, quote*(1-adverse)); when quote>=lp (marketable sell) adverse pushes quote down, and max(lp, lower) returns lp — fine. The real bug: a buy limit at exactly quote*(1+adverse) boundary can fill ABOVE the limit price is prevented by min, good — but adverse can make a marketable buy fill at quote*(1+adverse) which may be > lp when quote is just under lp, violating the limit guarantee.
fix: Cap the buy fill strictly at the limit: fill_price = min(lp, quote*(1+adverse)) already caps to lp, so this is fine; instead the genuine issue is the marketability test should use the slipped price, not raw quote — test `quote*(1+adverse) <= lp` for buys (and `quote*(1-adverse) >= lp` for sells) so a barely-marketable order that slips past the limit rests instead of filling beyond the limit.

title: PaperBroker holds per-instance _orders dict but get_broker constructs a NEW PaperBroker every call — get_order/cancel after submit see empty state
description: Each get_broker('paper') returns a fresh PaperBroker() with an empty self._orders. execute_trade does broker=get_broker(); submit; disconnect — fine within one call. But reconcile()/cancel_all_open() call get_broker again, get a NEW PaperBroker, and broker.get_order(boid)/cancel(boid) find nothing (state 'unknown'), so paper order resolution via the broker is broken. The system masks this because paper state is reconstructed from aj_fills, but get_order on the paper broker is effectively non-functional.
fix: Make PaperBroker order state durable (read from aj_orders/aj_fills) instead of an in-memory dict, or cache a singleton PaperBroker instance, so get_order/cancel work across get_broker calls.

title: cmd_secret takes the secret value as a CLI argument, exposing it in shell history and process listings
description: `secret --set scope=value` passes the plaintext credential on argv. It lands in shell history (~/.zsh_history), in `ps`/proc cmdline visible to other users, and possibly in CI logs. For a module whose entire purpose is encrypted-at-rest credential custody, accepting the secret on the command line undermines the threat model.
fix: Read the value from stdin or an env var / file path (e.g. `--set scope=@-` reads stdin, or `--from-file`), never directly from argv; at minimum support a getpass prompt.

title: Negative-guard loop silently rewrites a misconfigured cap to 0.0, which can mean 'block' OR 'unlimited' depending on the consumer
description: For every _FLOAT_KEYS entry, a negative stored value is forced to 0.0. For caps like max_order_notional_usd, 0.0 means 'block' (safe). But several float keys treat 0.0 as 'disabled/unlimited' (e.g. max_slippage_bps, take_profit_pct, max_symbol_weight_pct, risk_off_vix). A negative value (operator typo or bad migration) for, say, max_slippage_bps becomes 0.0 = 'feature off', silently removing a protective limit instead of failing closed.
fix: For protective limits where 0=disabled, clamp negatives to the DEFAULTS value (which is the safe/blocking value) rather than to 0.0; or reject the update at set_config time. At minimum, document and split the two semantics so a negative never disables a guard.

title: Lease-lock fallback has a cross-process TOCTOU and never closes the FD path
description: _acquire_lease() reads the lease then writes it under db._write_lock, but that lock is in-process only. Two separate processes (the exact scenario SingleInstanceLock exists to prevent) can both read an expired/absent lease and both write their own lease, so both 'acquire' the operator lock and run a cycle concurrently. This defeats single-instance protection on platforms without fcntl.
fix: Make the lease write conditional/atomic: use an INSERT with a uniqueness guard or a compare-and-set UPDATE (e.g. UPDATE ... WHERE key=? AND value=<old>), re-reading rowcount; only return True if exactly this process won the write. Alternatively gate on an OS-level atomic create (open(path, 'x')).

title: broker.disconnect() is skipped on any submit exception, leaking live broker connections
description: connect() is called, then submit(); if submit() raises, control jumps to the except blocks which set state but NEVER call broker.disconnect(). For live adapters that hold a session/socket, this leaks the connection on every failed submit. PaperBroker is a no-op, but the live path (the dangerous one) leaks.
fix: Wrap the submit in try/finally that always calls broker.disconnect() (best-effort), or move disconnect into a finally block covering the whole broker interaction.

title: reconcile live-halt decision keys on broker.mode but get_broker forces PaperBroker when live is off — divergence on a real live venue mislabeled
description: is_live = broker.mode=='live'. But reconcile() with venue=None calls get_broker(None) which, when live_trading_enabled is off, returns a PaperBroker (mode='paper'). If a divergence occurs it will never halt because is_live is False — acceptable for paper. However the comment claims 'default to treating uncertain mode as live (fail-closed)'; the code does the opposite (treats blank/unknown mode as NOT live), so a broker object with an unset mode attribute silently skips the live halt.
fix: Make is_live fail-closed as documented: `is_live = str(getattr(broker,'mode','live')).strip().lower() != 'paper'` so any non-'paper'/unknown mode is treated as live for the halt decision.

title: cancel_all_open marks an order canceled LOCALLY even when the live broker.cancel raised
description: In the try block, broker.cancel(boid) is attempted, then _set_state(oid,'canceled') and n+=1. If broker.cancel raises, control jumps to except and the order is NOT marked canceled (good). But if broker.cancel returns without raising yet the venue did not actually cancel (broker returns a non-canceled state), the code still marks the order canceled locally and counts it — diverging local state from a still-open live order, the exact hazard kill_switch's 'still_open' count is meant to catch but which this masks by flipping local state to canceled.
fix: Only mark canceled locally after confirming the broker.cancel result state is 'canceled'/terminal; otherwise set 'unknown' and leave for reconciliation, so kill_switch's still-open count reflects reality.

title: serve_stdio closure binds tool name correctly but registers tools with NO input schema, so MCP clients cannot pass args (symbol/limit/horizon)
description: server.tool(name=..., description=...)(_make(name)) wraps a `def _call(**kwargs)` with no typed signature. FastMCP derives the input schema from the function signature; a bare **kwargs exposes no parameters, so read tools that REQUIRE args (quote needs 'symbol', forecast_ensemble needs 'symbol'/'horizon_days', aj_proposals/aj_orders take 'limit', aj_positions takes 'mode') become uncallable with arguments over MCP — quote/forecast will always return {'error':'symbol required'}.
fix: Give each registered tool an explicit parameter signature (or attach an inputSchema) matching the args it reads, e.g. generate per-tool wrappers with named params, so FastMCP advertises the correct schema.

title: cumulative_pnl indexes p["avg_cost"] and p["qty"] without guards inside the try
description: unreal += (mark - p['avg_cost']) * p['qty']. If a position dict from paper_book lacks avg_cost/qty (or they are None), this raises KeyError/TypeError. It is inside a try/except that logs and continues, so unrealized silently becomes whatever partial sum accrued before the error — understating cumulative P&L without any visible failure, and the loop aborts mid-way leaving later positions uncounted.
fix: Use float(p.get('avg_cost') or 0) and float(p.get('qty') or 0), and continue per-symbol on bad data rather than aborting the whole loop (wrap the body, not the whole loop, or use .get).

title: FIFO sell lot-exhaustion uses lot[0] <= _EPS which prematurely drops a tiny-but-real remaining long lot
description: After consuming a long lot, `if lot[0] <= _EPS: dq.popleft()`. A positive long lot whose remaining qty is between 0 and _EPS (1e-9) is popped and its residual cost basis discarded. For a buy lot the residual should only be dropped when essentially zero; using <= _EPS on a strictly-positive quantity silently loses up to 1e-9 shares of basis each partial. Symmetric issue with `lot[0] >= -_EPS` on the cover side.
fix: Pop only when abs(lot[0]) <= _EPS (i.e. the lot is fully consumed within epsilon), not when it merely dropped below +_EPS while still positive; keep the residual lot otherwise.

title: avg_cost computed as cost/tot_qty mixes long and short lots, producing a meaningless average for a net position with both signs
description: positions are netted by summing all lot qtys and all lot costs. If a symbol's deque somehow holds both long and short lots (e.g. after interleaved fills with epsilon residuals not fully covered), tot_qty and cost can have opposing signs, making avg_cost = cost/tot_qty a nonsensical (possibly negative) number that then drives unrealized P&L and exit rules.
fix: After FIFO netting the deque should be single-signed; assert/guard that all lots share the sign of tot_qty, and if not, collapse properly. At minimum compute avg_cost as cost/tot_qty only when all lots are same-signed, else flag a data-quality warning.

title: paper_book books full fill fee into realized even for fills that only OPEN a position (no close)
description: realized = -fees is applied to realized_total/realized_today for EVERY fill, including pure opening buys that close nothing. So opening a brand-new long immediately shows a realized loss equal to the fee, inflating realized_today and pushing day_pnl toward the daily-loss HALT even though no position was closed. Open-position entry fees should be carried in cost basis, not realized.
fix: Only realize fees on the closing portion of a fill (as realized_trades attempts via closed_qty), and add opening-fill fees to the lot cost basis rather than realized_total/realized_today.

title: Session-open unrealized snapshot is never cleared, leaking one settings row per ET day forever
description: _session_open_unrealized writes key '__aj_unreal_open_<DATE>' once per ET day and never deletes prior days. Over time the settings table accumulates one row per trading day indefinitely. More subtly, get_settings() shallow-copies all rows on cache refresh, so this unbounded growth slowly bloats every settings read.
fix: After stamping today's key, opportunistically DELETE settings rows whose key matches '__aj_unreal_open_%' and whose date suffix != _session_date(); or prune in a retention job.

title: Session-open unrealized baseline is captured on first call regardless of whether it is actually session open
description: The 'open' baseline is whatever the unrealized happens to be on the first compute_day_pnl call of the ET day. If the first cycle of the day runs at, say, 2pm after a large drawdown already occurred, that drawdown is baked into unreal_open and excluded from day_pnl — defeating the daily-loss HALT it is meant to feed. The baseline should be captured at/near actual session open, not first observation.
fix: Capture/refresh the baseline only when market_session()=='premarket' or at the first 'regular' tick, and persist a session-open timestamp; if the first observation of the day is mid-session, fall back to a 0 baseline or to the prior close so accumulated drawdown is not silently excluded.

title: _project_pulse indexes book['positions'] directly, KeyError if paper_book returns a malformed dict
description: book = aj_positions.paper_book(); then `book['positions']` is accessed with subscripting (lines 242-243) instead of book.get('positions'). compute_day_pnl uses .get with a fallback, but _project_pulse assumes the key exists. If paper_book() ever returns a dict without 'positions' (e.g. a future error path returning {}), this raises KeyError, which propagates into _ips_block_reason's except and blocks the trade — fail-closed but mislabeled as an 'IPS check error'.
fix: Use book.get('positions') or {} on lines 242-243, mirroring compute_day_pnl's defensive access.

title: Daily-loss HALT comparison treats max_loss<=0 as an immediate halt, but the operator never re-arms automatically
description: `if not (max_loss > 0 and pnl['day_pnl'] > -max_loss)` halts whenever max_daily_loss_usd is 0 (the DEFAULT per aj_config). So with default config every proposal that reaches step 7 triggers halt() (disabling trading globally) rather than simply blocking. A 0 cap should mean 'block this order', not 'HALT all trading and disable the master switch'. This conflates a missing-config block with a loss-breach halt.
fix: When max_loss<=0, _record a 'block' (no usable daily-loss cap configured) and return a block decision instead of calling halt(); only halt when max_loss>0 AND day_pnl <= -max_loss.

title: _order_price ignores asset_type so crypto market orders get no quote and are blocked
description: evaluate() calls _order_price(symbol, order_type, limit_price) WITHOUT passing asset_type (the param defaults to ''). For a crypto symbol like 'BTC' that needs the -USD suffix, _quote_symbol(symbol,'') returns 'BTC' unchanged, so the crypto fallback quote lookup never happens and price is None -> every crypto market order is blocked as 'no quote'. The asset_type plumbing exists but is not threaded through here.
fix: Pass an inferred asset_type: `_order_price(symbol, order_type, limit_price, aj_positions.infer_asset_type(symbol))` (import lazily), so the -USD fallback in _order_price actually fires for crypto.

title: Unrealized P&L mixes crypto/stock without verifying the mark corresponds to the held symbol's quote convention
description: In compute_day_pnl, marks=_marks(syms) is keyed on the stored symbol; for crypto stored as 'BTC' (infer_asset_type still 'crypto' only if -USD/hint), the first _marks lookup uses 'BTC' which may resolve to an equity ticker 'BTC' quote rather than the crypto quote, producing a wildly wrong mark and bogus unrealized P&L that feeds the daily-loss halt.
fix: For each position, derive the quote symbol via _quote_symbol(sym, p.get('asset_type')) BEFORE the batch quote call and key marks on the resolved quote symbol, instead of trying the raw symbol first.

title: Daily-loss halt computes pnl with cfg.get('daily_loss_basis') but compute_day_pnl already defaults that internally — passing None vs the resolved basis is fine, yet halt fires AFTER all other gates, so a loss-breaching order is fully evaluated and only the LAST step halts
description: Step 7 (daily loss) runs after notional, trades/day, IPS, and enhanced gates. If trading should be HALTED due to an existing daily loss, the system still does all prior work and, crucially, a proposal that was going to be blocked for another reason never reaches step 7, so the HALT is not triggered even though the account is already in breach. The halt is order-dependent and can be skipped by an unrelated earlier block.
fix: Evaluate the daily-loss/halt condition EARLY (right after the master-switch/session checks) so an account already in breach halts regardless of the specific proposal, rather than only when a proposal happens to pass all other gates first.

title: PRIVATE 'escalation' retries the identical local model with identical params — not a real escalation
description: For sensitivity==PRIVATE, on a quality-floor miss the code retries _ollama_chat with exactly the same messages/max_tokens/temperature. A deterministic-ish local model given identical input is overwhelmingly likely to return the same (still-failing) output, so escalated=1 is recorded but the retry adds latency without any chance of crossing the floor. The spec intent ('bounded escalation') is not met.
fix: On the private retry, change a parameter that can affect output (e.g., raise temperature, or increase max_tokens like the public path does) so the retry has a genuine chance to pass the floor; otherwise skip the retry.

title: Trailing-stop uses peak that may be stale/below mark, and mixes with TP/SL via elif
description: In exit_signals the trailing branch is reached only via elif after tp/sl. peak = float((state.get(sym) or {}).get('peak_mark') or mark). If peak_mark is NULL/0 it defaults to mark, so (peak-mark)/peak = 0 and trailing never fires on the first cycle after open — acceptable. But because update_position_state runs separately, on the very cycle a position is opened there may be no state row yet, so peak==mark and trailing is silently disabled until the next cycle's state refresh. More concretely, if peak_mark wasn't refreshed this cycle (mark rose), the trailing distance is computed against a stale lower peak, under-reporting the drawdown from peak and missing the stop.
fix: Ensure update_position_state runs (and peak_mark is refreshed to include the current mark) before exit_signals each cycle, or compute peak = max(persisted_peak, mark) inside exit_signals so the trailing distance uses an up-to-date peak.

title: Slippage-guard estimate formula is nonsensical (spread fraction * 8)
description: est = paper_slippage_bps + 0.5 * paper_spread_fraction * 8. paper_spread_fraction is a fraction of the spread (e.g. 0.5), so 0.5*0.5*8 = 2.0 — a magic '8' multiplier with no units relation to bps. The spread component should be converted to bps using an actual spread estimate (spread/price*1e4), not a hard-coded 8. As written the guard compares an arbitrary number against max_slippage_bps and will block or pass essentially at random relative to real slippage.
fix: Compute the spread contribution in bps properly, e.g. est = paper_slippage_bps + 0.5 * paper_spread_fraction * estimated_spread_bps, deriving estimated_spread_bps from the quote (bid/ask) rather than the literal 8.

title: update_position_state read-then-write across lock boundary (check-then-act race)
description: existing = aj_db.query(...) is read OUTSIDE db_lock(); the lock is then acquired and rows are INSERT/UPDATE based on the stale `existing` snapshot. Between the read and the locked write, another writer (a fill applied in a concurrent cycle/thread) can change aj_position_state, so opened_at/peak_mark decisions are made on stale data — e.g. a position that just opened may be treated as existing-without-opened_at, or a peak update can clobber a concurrently-written higher peak.
fix: Move the existing-rows SELECT inside the `with db_lock():` block (read and write under the same lock) so the check-then-act is atomic.

title: lease() returns None indistinguishably for 'absent', 'read error', and 'decrypt error' — fail-closed, but masks key corruption
description: On a decrypt failure (e.g., the master key changed / blob corrupted) lease() logs and returns None — identical to 'secret not stored'. Callers (aj_alpaca._lease_keys) raise BrokerNotEnabled('could not lease keys (expired/missing)'), so a genuine key-mismatch disaster (all stored secrets undecryptable) is reported to the operator as merely 'missing', hiding a serious credential-custody failure that needs different remediation (re-key) than a missing secret.
fix: Distinguish the cases: keep returning None for absent, but on a decrypt exception either raise or return a sentinel/log at error level with a distinct marker so monitoring/operator can tell 'corrupt/rekeyed' from 'never stored'.

title: Sell sizing caps qty at target/price, under-selling exits driven by notional cap
description: For sells: qty = min(held_qty, target/price). `target` is the order_notional_target (default half the per-order cap), so an exit is limited to that notional even when the strategy intends to close the full position (exit_signals passes full qty downstream, but size_order independently recomputes qty from notional). A position worth more than `target` will only be partially sold, leaving residual risk the exit rule meant to remove.
fix: For sells, size to held_qty (the requested exit qty) rather than the notional target, e.g. qty = held_qty when side=='sell' and an explicit exit qty is provided; only apply the notional cap to buys.

title: High-risk regex matches substrings inside benign words, misclassifying read commands as high-risk
description: _HIGH_RISK uses \b(buy|sell|...|set|live|...)\b but is applied to the raw spoken text BEFORE read-intent matching. Words like 'set' appear in many benign read phrases, and 'live' in 'how are we doing, are we live?' Worse, the gate runs first (line 40) and short-circuits, so a status question containing any high-risk token (e.g. 'should I buy?' which is actually a private advisory read) is forced into the confirm-request branch and never reaches the read tools — and conversely a phrase like 'how much profit' is fine, but 'how much should I sell to...' is blocked. The ordering means read intents that legitimately mention these verbs can never be answered.
fix: Run read-intent matching first for pure read phrases, or tighten _HIGH_RISK to require an imperative/action context; at minimum, only treat high-risk verbs as blocking when no read intent matched.

title: Cannot clear a position's account_id via PUT /api/portfolio/<id>
description: The route deliberately normalizes an empty/null account_id to Python None (lines 572-574) intending to UN-assign the holding from its account. But db.update_position(account_id=None) treats None as 'leave unchanged' (database.py:530: new_acct = account_id if account_id is not None else pos['account_id']). So a user who moves a holding to 'No account' silently keeps the old account_id. The clear-account feature is broken.
fix: Distinguish 'omitted' from 'explicit clear'. In the route, only pass account_id to db.update_position when the key is present in data; and add a sentinel (e.g. account_id=0 meaning clear, or a separate clear_account flag) so db.update_position can set NULL. Minimal: change db.update_position to accept a sentinel like account_id=-1 for 'unchanged' and treat None as 'set NULL', then have the route pass -1 when 'account_id' not in data.

title: Institutional-holding overlap match produces false positives for short tickers
description: intel_institutional matches a portfolio symbol against a fund holding name with `if sym in h_name or h_name.startswith(sym)` (line 1629). For short/common tickers this matches unrelated names: ticker 'A' matches every holding whose name contains 'A'; 'V' matches 'VISA' but also 'NVIDIA'/'CHEVRON'; 'ON' matches 'EXXON'. The overlap_with_portfolio list is thus polluted with bogus matches, misreporting which funds hold the user's positions.
fix: Match on word boundaries / the holding's own ticker field instead of substring, e.g. require `sym == h.get('ticker','').upper()` when the holding carries a ticker, else use a regex word-boundary check `re.search(r'\\b'+re.escape(sym)+r'\\b', h_name)` and drop the `sym in h_name` substring test.

title: _safe spawns a new thread per warm call; orphaned slow calls leak threads and DB connections unbounded
description: Each warm call runs in a fresh daemon thread joined for WARM_CALL_TIMEOUT (45s). If the upstream blocks longer, the loop moves on but the orphaned thread keeps running and holds its thread-local DB/cache connections (never closed). Under a persistently-slow upstream the warmer creates a new orphan thread every cadence, accumulating threads and SQLite WAL-reader connections that in turn prevent VACUUM. There is no cap on concurrent orphans.
fix: Have _runner close thread-local connections in finally (database.close_thread_conn(); cache_store.close_thread_conn()); track/limit outstanding orphan threads and skip launching new warm calls of the same label while a prior one is still alive.

title: Thread-local DB connections are never closed for request/pool threads
description: get_conn() caches a sqlite3 connection on threading.local and only close_thread_conn() releases it. Flask/worker threads in a thread pool are long-lived and rotate; each distinct thread that ever calls get_conn() holds a connection FD for the life of the thread, and connections opened on threads that exit without calling close_thread_conn() leak the FD until GC. Under a server with many worker threads this accumulates open SQLite handles against wealth.db (WAL readers), which also blocks vacuum_db()/VACUUM (it returns -1 when readers are active). The warmer's per-call helper threads (cache_warmer._safe spawns a thread per warm call) never call close_thread_conn(), so every warm call that touches the DB leaks a connection.
fix: Have cache_warmer._safe's _runner call database.close_thread_conn() and cache_store.close_thread_conn() in its finally; and/or register a teardown that closes the thread-local conn when pooled threads finish a request.

title: add_position over-sell guard missing for brand-new (no existing row) sell
description: add_position only validates `total_shares < 0` when an existing row is found. If a SELL (shares<0) arrives for a symbol with NO existing position, the `else` (insert) branch runs and inserts a portfolio row with negative shares and avg_cost set to the SELL price — creating a phantom short position with corrupted basis. The over-sell protection the function documents only covers the average-down path.
fix: Before the insert branch, reject negative-share inserts: `if shares < 0: raise ValueError('Cannot sell shares of a position not held')` (or skip the insert).

title: save_snapshot keyed on date but schema lacks PRIMARY KEY — INSERT OR REPLACE can't dedupe
description: portfolio_snapshots declares `date TEXT UNIQUE` (line 152) but no PRIMARY KEY. INSERT OR REPLACE relies on a UNIQUE/PK conflict to overwrite. UNIQUE on date does trigger REPLACE, so dedupe works — UNLESS date is NULL (UNIQUE allows multiple NULLs in SQLite), in which case every NULL-date snapshot inserts a new row, growing unbounded. save_snapshot trusts the caller to pass a non-null date; a caller passing None silently breaks the once-per-day contract and the prune_portfolio_snapshots month-keep logic (which filters `date IS NOT NULL`).
fix: Reject/guard NULL date in save_snapshot: `if not date: date = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime('%Y-%m-%d')` before the INSERT.

title: Annualized return uses arithmetic-mean compounding — wildly overstates return
description: `ann_return = (1 + r.mean())**252 - 1` compounds the simple daily mean return 252 times. For volatile series this massively overstates annualized return (Jensen's-gap / volatility drag is ignored), and for a symbol with a large positive mean it can report absurd figures (e.g. thousands of percent). The metric feeds the risk panel and Calmar ratio, so the displayed annualized_return and calmar_ratio are both materially wrong.
fix: Use the geometric (CAGR) form consistent with total_return already computed below: `ann_return = ((1 + r).prod() ** (trading_days / len(r)) - 1) * 100`, or annualize the log-mean. At minimum document/divide so it is geometric rather than (1+mean)^252.

title: Finviz fallback sets change_pct from 'Change' but change is recomputed from prev — sign/zero mismatch and prev may be missing
description: In _finviz_quote_fallback, `chg_pct = _num(fund.get('Change'))` is Finviz's reported % change, while `chg` is recomputed as `price - prev`. If Finviz omits 'Prev Close' (common for ETF proxies/indices), `prev` is None so `chg` becomes None while `chg_pct` is a real number — the UI then shows a percent move with no absolute change, and prev_close=None breaks downstream P/L math. Worse, the two fields can disagree in sign because chg_pct comes from a different field than the recomputed chg.
fix: When prev is None but price and chg_pct are present, derive prev from chg_pct: `prev = price/(1+chg_pct/100) if (price is not None and chg_pct is not None) else prev` before computing chg, so change/prev_close/change_pct are mutually consistent.

title: Crypto quote lookup uses uppercased key but stock path does not, inconsistency risk
description: In _portfolio_pulse, crypto quotes are stored under `prices[sym]` keyed by the bare symbol, fetched via cq.get((sym+'-USD').upper()). Later `q = prices.get(h["symbol"], {})`. This works only if h['symbol'] exactly matches the bare sym used as key (it does, both from holdings). However get_quotes_batch for stocks returns UPPERCASE keys; prices.update(...) inserts uppercase keys, and h['symbol'] is uppercase from DB, so OK. The real bug: if a holding symbol is stored lowercase anywhere, the stock-quote lookup misses. Low risk given DB uppercases, but the crypto branch and stock branch use different keying conventions making this fragile.
fix: Normalize: use `q = prices.get(h["symbol"].upper(), {})` consistently so any casing mismatch can't silently drop a position from the pulse.

title: day_pnl_pct divides by prev_value which can be near zero or negative
description: `prev_value = total_value - day_pnl; ...day_pnl/prev_value*100 if (day_pnl_known and prev_value)`. prev_value is only guarded against being falsy (exact 0). If prev_value is a tiny positive number (e.g. a day where the book nearly doubled) or negative (impossible for long-only but possible with bad data), the percentage explodes to absurd values that then reach the headline ('Portfolio up 4000% today'). The guard `and prev_value` doesn't protect against tiny/negative denominators.
fix: Guard `prev_value > 0` (and optionally a minimum magnitude) before computing the percentage; else return None.

title: Near-alert distance uses (level-price)/price giving wrong sign logic for 'below' alerts
description: In _alert_insights, `dist_pct=(level-price)/price*100`. For an 'above' alert the near test is `0<dist_pct<=2` (price just under level — correct). For 'below' it's `0<-dist_pct<=2`, i.e. dist_pct negative meaning level<price (price just above the level — correct). This is actually right, BUT the message always prints `abs(dist_pct)` and `level` with alert_type — fine. The real issue: dist_pct is computed relative to price, so 'within 2%' is measured against current price not the level; for a 'below' alert deep moves this skews the threshold. Minor semantic, but the bigger bug is `if not price or not level` rejects a legitimate level of 0; unlikely for alerts though.
fix: Compute distance relative to the alert level for symmetry: `dist_pct=(level-price)/level*100`, and guard `price is None or level is None` rather than truthiness.

title: Forecast hit-rate display double-converts when hr is a percentage
description: _forecast_line: `hr*100 if hr<=1 else hr` is used both in the format and the >=55 comparison. If hr arrives as 0.58 it becomes 58 (good); if it arrives as 58 it stays 58 (good). But the threshold compares the SAME expression — consistent. The real defect: the n used is `(ens.get('calibration') or {}).get('n')` while hr is from track_record; these can be different sample sizes, so the sentence 'X% over N calls' pairs a hit-rate with an unrelated calibration N.
fix: Take n from the same track_record block as hr (rec.get('n_directional') / tr.get('n')), not from calibration, so the rate and count describe the same sample.

title: _answer_range divides by lo and hi without re-checking after _finite already passed but price could be 0
description: _answer_range: hi/lo validated via _finite and hi>lo, but `price=q["price"]` is taken raw (the earlier guard only checked q.get('price') is None). `above_lo=(price-lo)/lo*100` divides by lo; lo>0 guaranteed by `not lo` check (lo truthy) so lo!=0 — ok. `off_hi=(hi-price)/hi*100` divides by hi (truthy) — ok. So no ZeroDivision. However price is not run through _finite, so a NaN/inf price would propagate into pos/off_hi/above_lo and format as 'nan'. The quote guard only checks price is None, not finiteness.
fix: Run `price=_finite(q.get('price'))` and bail if None, mirroring other answer helpers.

title: _FORGET_RE allows up to 9-digit id but int() then jarvis_delete_memory with huge id is fine; however m.group on second branch
description: _answer_memory forget path: `mem_id=int(m.group(1))`. _FORGET_RE is `^forget\s+(?:#|memory\s*)?(\d{1,9})$` — single group, so group(1) exists. Fine. But the success message uses m.group(1) again after possibly deleting — ok. The genuine bug: there is no upper bound sanity and int of 9 digits is fine. Lower severity; the actual risk is jarvis_delete_memory(mem_id) for a non-existent id returns False and message is correct. Reclassifying: no crash. Removing concern.
fix: No fix needed; id is bounded by regex.

title: _corrections_table / _log_correction use db._write_lock + get_conn without ensuring connection thread-safety
description: _corrections_table acquires db._write_lock and calls db.get_conn().execute(...).commit(). _answer_corrections_learned (line 4083-4089) calls _corrections_table() then get_conn() WITHOUT the write lock for the SELECT. If get_conn returns a per-thread connection this is fine, but reading immediately after a CREATE on a possibly different connection without the lock can race with concurrent writers, and the read path holds no lock during fetchall, risking 'database is locked' under concurrency.
fix: Wrap the readback in the same db._write_lock (or a read lock) as the table-create, or use a dedicated helper that serializes access consistent with the rest of database.py.

title: _PENDING_CLARIFY global dict mutated without a lock across request threads
description: _PENDING_CLARIFY is a module-level dict read/written by ask() (line 4313, 4356-4359) and _set_pending_clarify (4120-4125) from concurrent Flask request threads. The opportunistic GC iterates and pops while another thread may insert, and the check-then-pop in ask() (`pend=_PENDING_CLARIFY.get; ...pop`) is a non-atomic check-then-act. Under concurrency this can raise 'dictionary changed size during iteration' in the GC loop or lose/duplicate clarify state across conversations.
fix: Guard all _PENDING_CLARIFY access with a module-level threading.Lock, and snapshot keys with list() before iterating in the GC (the GC already does list-comp, but the insert under the same lock is missing).

title: Biggest 'relief' selected with min() picks most-negative delta but labels saving wrong on ties/zero
description: reliefs are rows with delta<0. best = min(reliefs, key=delta_usd) correctly finds the largest-magnitude saving, but _usd(best['delta_usd']) formats abs() so it's fine. The real bug: a 'relief' can have delta exactly at the negative wash boundary edge already filtered, so OK — however the regret branch uses max(...delta_usd) which is correct, but when ALL rows are 'wash' AND net is computed from raw deltas, the lead says 'washes, all of them' yet tail may say 'cost X'/'saved X' because net sums tiny sub-band deltas that can exceed $1 in aggregate. The lead and tail then contradict (e.g. 'washes, all of them. Net, the urge to sell has cost $40').
fix: Make the wash-band classification and the net narrative consistent: compute net only over non-wash rows, or gate the tail wording on whether any non-wash verdicts exist (if no regrets and no reliefs, force the wash tail regardless of net).

title: min() over mixed None/str first-buy dates raises TypeError
description: first = min(t.get('date') or t.get('created_at', '') for t in buys). If a BUY row has date=None AND created_at missing, the generator yields '' for it, but if date is None and created_at is None (column present but null), t.get('created_at','') returns None (key exists with null value), so the generator can yield None alongside strings. min() of mixed None and str raises TypeError: '<' not supported between 'NoneType' and 'str'. The surrounding try/except (line 220) catches it, but then first_buy/holding_days are silently dropped for the whole ownership block even though the data was fine.
fix: Coerce to string and filter falsy: dates = [str(t.get('date') or t.get('created_at') or '') for t in buys]; dates = [d for d in dates if d]; first = min(dates) if dates else None; guard the rest on `if first:`.

title: Chase detection uses price/shares without None/type guards; arithmetic on None or strings
description: price = t.get('price') or 0 and sh = t.get('shares') or 0 then `price > (cost_total/cost_shares)*(1+...)` and `cost_total += price*sh`. If price/shares come back as strings (some import paths store text), the comparison/multiplication raises TypeError or compares str to float, which is silently swallowed only if wrapped — but this loop is NOT inside a try/except, so a single string price aborts the entire chase-detection block (and any observations after it in _temperament_uncached) — actually it propagates to the outer caller. _temperament_uncached has no top-level try around this section.
fix: Coerce with _num: p = _num(t.get('price')); s = _num(t.get('shares')); skip the row when either is None. This matches the defensive coercion used elsewhere and prevents a bad row from crashing the temperament check.

title: SELL average-cost reduction loses cost basis: cost_total = avg*remaining double-applies avg
description: On SELL: avg = cost_total/cost_shares; cost_shares = max(0, cost_shares - sh); cost_total = avg*cost_shares. This RESETS cost_total to avg*remaining, which is correct ONLY if avg is unchanged — but it silently discards any record that the remaining lot's true cost differs (it's an average book, so acceptable). The real defect: if sh > cost_shares (oversell / imported sell without buy), cost_shares clamps to 0, cost_total becomes 0, and a subsequent BUY then re-establishes basis from scratch — but the prior basis is wiped, so a later legitimate chase against the old basis is missed. Also if cost_shares becomes 0, the next BUY's chase check `cost_shares > 0` is False so the first re-buy is never flagged.
fix: Only reduce basis proportionally and don't zero it on partial sells; guard oversells by not letting cost_total go negative but preserve average when cost_shares>0. The clamp logic is acceptable for averages but document that oversells reset basis; at minimum ensure cost_total stays consistent: cost_total = avg * cost_shares is fine, leave as is but coerce inputs (see prior finding).

title: _ensure_table calls db.get_conn() twice; second call may return a different connection than committed
description: with db._write_lock: db.get_conn().execute(_TABLE_SQL); db.get_conn().commit(). If get_conn() returns per-thread or new connections, execute() runs on one connection and commit() on another, so the DDL may never be committed (or committed on a connection with no pending transaction). The same double-get_conn anti-pattern repeats in store(), forget(), recall(), index_memories(), stats().
fix: Bind once: conn = db.get_conn(); conn.execute(_TABLE_SQL); conn.commit(). Apply the single-handle pattern to every function that currently calls db.get_conn() more than once in the same block.

title: stress_test mutates the live portfolio holding dicts in place
description: _t_stress_test iterates `for h in holdings: h["market_value"]=...; h["current_price"]=...` directly on the list returned by db.get_portfolio(). If get_portfolio() returns cached/shared dict rows, these writes pollute the shared objects with derived fields, and the per-call mutation can leak into other readers. Even if rows are fresh, it also accesses h["asset_type"] (line 267-268) and h["avg_cost"]/h["shares"] (line 280-281) by hard index, raising KeyError if any holding lacks those keys, aborting the whole tool.
fix: Copy each row before annotating (e.g. `h = dict(h)` into a new list) and use h.get("asset_type") / h.get("avg_cost",0) / h.get("shares",0) defensively, passing the copied list to get_portfolio_stress_test.

title: add_alert calls float(args.get('price')) which raises TypeError on None
description: _t_add_alert does `price = float(args.get("price"))`. If the confirmed args omit price or send null, float(None) raises TypeError. While valid_proposal_args guards the proposal path, execute_mutating (and execute_mutating_batch) re-validate via valid_proposal_args first, but execute_mutating() itself does NOT call valid_proposal_args — it directly runs the fn. A direct execute_mutating('add_price_alert', {...}) with a missing price raises TypeError, caught and returned as a raw error string. Inconsistent with _t_add_holding which uses _trade_price/_num_arg.
fix: Use `price = _num_arg(args.get('price'))` and raise ValueError('price required') when None, mirroring _trade_price.

title: execute_mutating does not validate args before executing
description: execute_mutating() only checks the tool is mutating, then calls spec['fn'](args). It does NOT call valid_proposal_args. So if /api/jarvis/act calls execute_mutating directly with attacker- or model-supplied args that passed an earlier (possibly stale) confirm, malformed args reach the executor and rely on each fn's internal guards. add_price_alert (float(None) TypeError) and others differ in robustness. The batch path validates; the single path does not — an inconsistency that can let malformed actions through.
fix: Add `if not valid_proposal_args(name, args): return {'error':'invalid arguments'}` at the top of execute_mutating, mirroring execute_mutating_batch.

title: change_pct watches on non-held coins never get -USD fallback, so crypto day-change always False
description: _fetch_quotes only retries SYM-USD when the bare quote's PRICE is missing/non-positive. A watch on change_pct for a coin the user doesn't hold (e.g. DOGE) may get a bare-ticker quote that returns a price (an unrelated equity named DOGE) but a wrong/absent change_pct, so no retry happens and the condition silently evaluates against the WRONG asset's change. Even when the bare ticker has no price (retry fires), _condition_holds reads change_pct from the retried -USD quote — fine — but when bare price exists the coin is mis-resolved.
fix: Drive the -USD retry off the metric being requested, or always retry SYM-USD for symbols that look crypto-shaped and prefer the -USD quote; minimally, also trigger retry when change_pct is missing for a change_pct watch, not only when price is missing.

title: evaluate_all updates rows under write lock but reads rows (line 381) outside it — TOCTOU on armed flag
description: Armed watches are SELECTed at line 381 with no lock, then network fetches happen (seconds), then updates run under db._write_lock at 417. If delete_watch or rearm_watch or another evaluate_all runs concurrently in that window, evaluate_all can stamp triggered_at=0 on a watch the user just deleted/rearmed, or two evaluators can both fire the same watch (double-trigger) because the armed=1 check at SELECT is stale by update time. The UPDATE has no 'WHERE armed=1' guard to make it idempotent.
fix: Add a guard to the trigger UPDATE: 'UPDATE jarvis_watches SET armed=0,... WHERE id=? AND armed=1' so a watch already disarmed/deleted between SELECT and UPDATE isn't re-triggered, and check cur.rowcount before appending to triggered.

title: ml_forecast module-level cache mutated without a lock (read/write race)
description: _forecast_cache and _cache_times are plain module dicts read at lines 526-529 and written at 630-631 with no lock. ml_forecast is invoked from forecast_ensemble via safe_executor.parallel_map (ThreadPoolExecutor) and from multiple Flask request threads concurrently. Concurrent training of the same symbol both write the dict; worse, a check-then-act on _cache_times can let many threads simultaneously run the 2-5s training (thundering herd), and partial dict updates are visible to readers. Other modules here correctly route through cache_store.coalesce (single-flight); this one does not.
fix: Guard cache reads/writes with a threading.Lock, or better route through cache_store.coalesce like the sibling modules so concurrent callers share one in-flight computation instead of each retraining.

title: Cached scan result mutated in place (result['scan_meta']['cached']=True) corrupts stored object
description: Both scan_opportunities (cache-hit branch) and get_cached_scan do `result = _scan_cache[phash]; result['scan_meta']['cached']=True; return result`. This mutates the cached dict itself, so the stored entry permanently has cached=True; a later code path or test that inspects the cached object sees cached=True even on what should be a fresh-compute return, and the same object is shared/returned to multiple callers (aliasing) so a caller mutating the returned dict corrupts the cache.
fix: Deep/shallow-copy before annotating: `result = dict(_scan_cache[phash]); result['scan_meta'] = dict(result['scan_meta']); result['scan_meta']['cached']=True`.

title: Horizon close looked up with calendar-day due date but horizon is documented as days
description: score_hypothesis computes due = created + timedelta(days=horizon) and prices the close at `due`. The hypothesis horizon_days is treated as calendar days here, while the sibling research_tracker.score_due_forecasts explicitly converts trading-day horizons to calendar days (ceil(h*7/5)). If hypothesis horizons are intended as trading days (consistent with the rest of AUGUR), the close is read ~28% short of the intended window, systematically mis-resolving CONFIRMED/REJECTED.
fix: If horizon_days is trading days, convert before computing due: `due = created + timedelta(days=math.ceil(horizon*7/5))`. If it is genuinely calendar days, leave as-is but document the divergence from the tracker. Confirm the intended unit and make both modules consistent.

title: Tracking-error uses uppercased symbols against original-case delta keys
description: compare_to_current builds delta keyed by syms (original case from current_weights/optimal_weights). _estimate_cov_and_mean returns `used` with symbols upper-cased (usable.append(s.upper())). The line `d = np.array([delta.get(s, 0.0) for s in used])` then looks up uppercased symbols in delta. If callers pass lowercase/mixed-case weight dicts, every lookup misses and d becomes all zeros, so tracking_error_pct is reported as 0.0 — a silently wrong risk number.
fix: Build delta with a normalized (upper) key, or look up case-insensitively: `d = np.array([delta.get(s, delta.get(s.upper(), 0.0)) for s in used])`. Cleanest: normalize syms to upper when constructing delta and accept weight dicts case-insensitively.

title: Score price uses chart bar even when due_at is far before earliest bar, fabricating a return
description: _close_price_on_or_before falls back to bars[0]['close'] (the OLDEST available bar) when target pre-dates all bars (line 230-231). In score_due_forecasts, score_price is the close at due_at; if the symbol's 2y chart window has rolled forward so that due_at is now older than the earliest bar (e.g. a long-dormant backlog finally scored), score_price silently becomes the oldest available close rather than the true horizon-end close, producing a meaningless realized return that is then committed as the row's score.
fix: In _close_price_on_or_before, only fall back to bars[0] when target is genuinely before bars[0] AND within a tolerance; otherwise return None so the scorer skips (errors+=1) rather than committing a fabricated price. Better: return None when no bar is <= target and let the caller decide.

title: Contagion ASSESS IMPACT calls wrong URL (404)
description: The frontend fetches `/api/contagion/${symbol}/impact`, but the Flask route is `/api/contagion/impact/<symbol>` (app.py line 1892). Every ASSESS IMPACT click hits a non-existent route, returns a 404/HTML error, and the feature is completely broken.
fix: Change the fetch to `API.get('/api/contagion/impact/' + symbol)` to match the registered route.

title: Contagion impact table reads wrong response keys
description: assess_contagion() returns `impacted_companies` (list) with per-item keys `impact_score` and `contagion_risk`. The JS reads `data.impacts || data.impact` (neither exists → empty), and per-row `imp.score`/`imp.risk_level` (wrong keys). Even if the URL were fixed, the impact table would render empty or with missing score/risk.
fix: Use `var impacts = data.impacted_companies || [];` and read `imp.impact_score` and `imp.contagion_risk` (keeping fallbacks if desired).

title: Contagion graph 'connected companies' never renders (wrong keys)
description: build_graph() returns the connections under `nodes`/`edges` (weight/revenue_pct/context live on `edges`), and the source company name under `company_name`. The JS reads `data.connections || data.connected_companies` (neither exists) so Total Connections shows 0 and the CONNECTED COMPANIES table never renders; `data.company` is also wrong (it's `company_name`).
fix: Build the connection rows from `data.edges` (joined with `data.nodes` for name/sector) or have the backend also emit a `connections` array; read `data.company_name` for the company KPI.

title: Reflexivity loop cards keyed by lowercase but backend types are uppercase
description: loopTypes use keys like `equity_feedback`; the code indexes `loops[lt.key]`. The backend loop objects carry `type` = `EQUITY_FEEDBACK`/`DILUTION_SPIRAL`/`INDEX_INCLUSION`/`SHORT_SQUEEZE` (uppercase), and `loops` is built as `loops[l.type]=l`. So `loops['equity_feedback']` is always undefined and every card shows Detected: NO with empty strength/direction — the exact bug the surrounding comment claims to have fixed.
fix: Match case, e.g. set `loopTypes` keys to uppercase (`EQUITY_FEEDBACK`, ...) or look up via `loops[lt.key.toUpperCase()]`.

title: Synthetic-insider CHANNEL BREAKDOWN never renders (dict vs array)
description: compute_composite() returns `channels` as a dict keyed by channel name (options_flow, volume_anomaly, ...). The JS does `var channels = data.channels || ...; if (channels.length)` — a dict has no `.length`, so the table is always skipped and per-channel detail is never shown.
fix: Convert the dict to an array, e.g. `var channels = Array.isArray(data.channels) ? data.channels : Object.entries(data.channels||{}).map(([k,v])=>Object.assign({channel:k}, v));`

title: Alt-data nowcast reads multiple wrong keys (beat prob/surprise/confidence/signals)
description: nowcast_revenue() returns `beat_probability` as a STRING ('LIKELY BEAT'/'UNCERTAIN'/'LIKELY MISS'), `estimated_surprise_pct` (not `estimated_surprise`), `confidence_level` (not `confidence`), and `signals` as a DICT. The JS treats beat_probability as a number (`>=60`, `_alphaFmtNum`), reads the wrong surprise/confidence keys (always '—'), and checks `signals.length` on a dict so SIGNAL BREAKDOWN never renders.
fix: Render `beat_probability` as a label string (badge by value), read `data.estimated_surprise_pct` and `data.confidence_level`, and convert `signals` dict to an array before the `.length`/loop.

title: _build_note divides by ratio without guarding ratio==0 → ZeroDivisionError path / and negative historical
description: _build_note computes `ratio = historical / implied` after guarding implied>0.01, then in the `ratio <= 0.8` branch computes `(1/ratio-1)*100`. If historical is 0.0 (a real, non-None value), ratio=0.0 and 1/ratio raises ZeroDivisionError, which is NOT caught here and propagates up through _make_event into the per-symbol worker (where it's caught and turns the whole event into an error). historical can legitimately be 0.0 from _historical_overlay when avg_abs_event_move_pct rounds to 0.
fix: Guard the expensive-premium branch: `elif ratio <= 0.8 and ratio > 0:` and add an explicit `ratio == 0` / historical≈0 case that returns a 'historical ~0' message instead of computing 1/ratio.

title: _c_price_momentum label format re-divides (hi-lo) without the float() guards used above → ZeroDivisionError when hi==lo passes truthiness
description: The label uses `((price-lo)/(hi-lo)) if (price and hi and lo and float(hi)>float(lo)) else 0.5`. The guard requires float(hi)>float(lo), so hi==lo is excluded — safe. But `price and hi and lo` treats a legitimate price/lo of 0.0 as falsy, diverging from the pieces computation above which used `is not None`. A genuine lo of 0 (e.g. a stock that hit 0 intraday is impossible, but a None-coerced 0) would fall to 0.5 inconsistently. Low-to-medium; the more pressing issue is the duplicated float() conversions can raise inside .format() if pct/price are non-numeric strings (not caught — the earlier try/except only wraps the pieces, not the label build).
fix: Compute the label numbers once inside the guarded try blocks (reuse the already-validated floats) instead of re-converting `float(pct)/float(price)/float(lo)/float(hi)` unguarded inside the .format() call; or wrap the label construction in its own try/except returning a plain '{n}' fallback.

title: Congress buy/sell classification misroutes Sale/Exchange via startswith('s')/('p')
description: In _congress_net_60d the combined `ttype = (txn_type + ' ' + txn_type_raw).lower().strip()` is tested with `ttype.startswith('p')` for buys and `ttype.startswith('s')` for sells. But ttype begins with the human label (e.g. 'sale s', 'purchase p', 'sell partial s'). For an Exchange row txn_type='Exchange' raw='E', ttype='exchange e' → starts with 'e', neither branch fires (acceptable). However a label like 'sale (exercise) se' starts with 's' (ok) but a raw-only row where txn_type is '' and raw='PE' gives 'pe' → startswith('p') → buy (ok). The real bug: when txn_type label is absent and raw='S...' the string is just the raw, but when label present 'sell' the code relies on substring 'sell' which is fine; the startswith fallback on the *combined* string keys off the label's first letter, so any future label starting with 'p'/'s' that is NOT a purchase/sale (e.g. 'split', 'pending') is silently miscounted. More concretely, the parallel synth_sectorflow._congress_index and synth_consensus._c_congress key off raw.startswith('P')/('S') on the RAW code only, which is correct; divmap keying off the combined-string first char is inconsistent and fragile.
fix: Mirror synth_consensus/_sectorflow: compute `raw = (t.get('txn_type_raw') or '').upper().strip()` and branch on `raw.startswith('P')` / `raw.startswith('S')` (plus the label substring checks), rather than `ttype.startswith('p')/('s')` on the combined lowercased label+raw string.

title: _close_series compares close 'c' with 0 before float() — TypeError if close is a non-numeric string
description: In _close_series the guard is `if c is None or t is None or c <= 0: continue` BEFORE `float(c)`. If get_chart_data returns close as a numeric string (e.g. '123.4') the comparison `c <= 0` does str <= int → TypeError on Python 3, which is uncaught inside the loop body's lack of try, crashing the whole series build (the outer try only wraps the fetch call, not the loop).
fix: Coerce first: wrap the body in try/except or do `cf = _to_float(c)`; `if cf is None or t is None or cf <= 0: continue` then `out[d] = cf`. Never compare a possibly-string close with an int.

title: _forward_return off-by-one: end_idx>=len rejects the last valid bar, and days uses index offset not calendar
description: _forward_return computes end_idx=start_idx+days and rejects when `end_idx >= len(sorted_dates)`. The last addressable index is len-1, so end_idx==len-1 is valid but the `>=` only rejects end_idx==len and above — that part is fine. The real issue: it returns None when end_idx >= len, i.e. when there aren't `days` MORE bars; combined with _FWD_DAYS the FactorFrame.forward_5d uses `end = i+5; if end > len` (allows end==len). The two forward-window helpers use inconsistent boundary tests (`>=` vs `>`), so price and factor 5d windows can include/exclude the final episode differently, biasing the averaged response.
fix: Make both consistent: price end_idx valid when end_idx <= len-1, i.e. reject only when `start_idx+days > len-1`. Align the factor-frame test (`end > len`) and the price test (`end_idx >= len`) to the same inclusive/exclusive convention.

title: Optimizer verdict compares proposed_size (fraction of proposed book) against optimal weight from a DIFFERENT symbol universe
description: markowitz_optimize runs on `symbols = current symbols ∪ {cand}` and returns optimal weights over THAT set. proposed_size is cand_mv/proposed_nav where proposed_nav is the user's actual book (which may include holdings not in the optimizer set if cleaning differs, and excludes nothing). The optimal weight is the optimizer's idealized allocation across only the union set with long_only/max_weight=1.0, not directly comparable to the user's actual position fraction of their full NAV. So OVERSIZED/UNDERSIZED verdicts compare apples (idealized weight in a constrained re-optimization) to oranges (actual fraction of current book). A user with cash or excluded assets gets systematically wrong verdicts.
fix: Compute proposed_size over the same symbol universe the optimizer used (sum of those symbols' MV), or explicitly normalize both to the optimizer's investable set, so the ratio compares like-for-like.

title: Scenario loss shift sign/comment inverted: losses are negative %, subtracting gives wrong 'worse=positive' semantics
description: _scenario_shifts: `out[k] = round(n - c, 4)` with comment 'Positive shift = proposed loses MORE (worse). Losses are already negative percentages, so subtract for delta.' If losses are negative (e.g. cur=-30, new=-40 means proposed loses more), n-c = -40-(-30) = -10 → NEGATIVE, contradicting the stated 'positive = worse'. The delta sign is inverted relative to the documented and UI-consumed convention.
fix: Flip to `c - n` (so more-negative new loss yields a positive 'worse' shift), or update the convention/labels consistently. Verify against how the UI colors the shift.

title: retry-after-ms detection uses k.endswith('-ms') but loop only checks 'retry-after-ms' last; value parse can use wrong unit
description: The loop iterates ('retry-after','Retry-After','retry-after-ms'). For a header dict that only has 'retry-after-ms', the first two .get return None, the third returns the ms value and ms=True so it divides by 1000 correctly. But if a case-insensitive header map returns the SAME value for 'retry-after' as for 'retry-after-ms' (because the map ignores case AND the '-ms' suffix differs only in suffix), it would read the ms value under the 'retry-after' key (ms=False) and treat milliseconds as seconds — a 2000ms wait becomes a 2000-second wait, clamped to RETRY_AFTER_CAP (60s). Unlikely with real maps but the unit detection is fragile.
fix: Detect the unit from the key actually matched explicitly and prefer the seconds header when both exist; only treat as ms when the matched key literally ends in '-ms'. Current code mostly does this; ensure the seconds keys are tried and returned before the -ms key (they are), so reorder is unnecessary — but add a guard that a numeric value > _GOV_RETRY_AFTER_CAP*1000 implies ms.

title: _rule_based_summarize calls text.lower() on possibly-None filing text
description: text_lower = text.lower() with no None guard. summarize_filing forwards filing_text straight through; if a caller passes None (no filing body fetched), this raises AttributeError, and unlike the OpenAI path there's no surrounding try/except in _rule_based_summarize, so it propagates to the caller and breaks the summary feature.
fix: text = text or ''; text_lower = text.lower(). Also guard text[:3000] re.findall accordingly.

title: Portfolio summary prompt subscripts summary['total_value'] etc. with format specs; None/missing crashes to fallback
description: user_prompt formats summary['total_value'] (:,.2f), summary['total_pnl'], summary['total_pnl_pct'], summary['total_cost'], summary['num_positions'] by direct subscript. If the caller's summary dict lacks any key or carries None, this raises KeyError/format TypeError, caught at 844 and silently degraded to rule-based — losing AI output. _rule_based uses .get with defaults, so the contracts are inconsistent.
fix: Use summary.get(...) with numeric defaults and pre-format, mirroring the defensive .get already used in _rule_based_portfolio_analysis.

title: _rule_based_portfolio_analysis subscripts p['symbol'] and set(p['asset_type']) — KeyError on incomplete holding
description: concentration loop and types=set(p['asset_type'] for p in holdings) and later position_insights p['symbol'] use direct subscripting. A holding missing 'asset_type' or 'symbol' raises KeyError; this function has no try/except, so the keyless fallback path crashes outright when given imperfect holdings — the exact scenario (no API key) where robustness matters most.
fix: Use p.get('asset_type') (filter None) and p.get('symbol','?'); guard the set comprehension against None asset types.

title: Earnings brief history/moves lines subscript r['date']/m['date']/m['move_pct'] inside list comps
description: history_lines uses r['date'], r['estimate'], r['actual']; moves_lines uses m['date'], m['move_pct'] with :+.2f. A history/move row missing 'date' (KeyError) or with move_pct None (format TypeError) raises inside _earnings_brief_uncached; caught at 1052 and degraded to rule-based, discarding the AI brief. The filter `if r.get('estimate') and r.get('actual')` guards estimate/actual but not 'date'.
fix: Use r.get('date','?'), m.get('date','?'), and coerce m.get('move_pct') with a None guard (skip rows whose move_pct isn't numeric) so one bad row doesn't sink the whole brief.

title: generate_idea_thesis cap-check-then-cache race serves stale or re-pays after midnight reset
description: When _cap_exceeded() is true it tries cache_store.cache_get(cache_key) and returns cached if present, else the cap envelope. But the cache_key includes round(float(idea.get('composite') or 0),1) and model; the cached entry may be the cap envelope itself from an earlier call (since _do_call stores its return into coalesce), so a transient cap can poison the cache with a cap envelope that then serves for the full 12h TTL even after the budget resets at midnight.
fix: Ensure cap envelopes are never written to the long-TTL cache: have _do_call return the cap envelope without coalesce caching it (cache_store should treat error-shaped envelopes as non-cacheable), or check cap and short-circuit BEFORE coalesce without storing the envelope under cache_key.

title: _fills_for iterates the activities response outside the try/except; a dict/error body raises AttributeError
description: The _request call is wrapped in try/except, but the `for a in (acts or [])` loop and the `a.get(...)` calls are outside it. Alpaca's activities endpoint normally returns a JSON list, but on some error/edge responses it returns a JSON object (dict). Iterating a dict yields its string keys, so `a.get(...)` becomes str.get → AttributeError, which propagates uncaught out of submit()/get_order() and crashes the order path that was supposed to merely enrich fills.
fix: Guard the response type: `if not isinstance(acts, list): return []` before the loop, or move the loop inside the existing try/except.

title: submit() always sends qty and time_in_force='day', breaking notional orders and limit TIF
description: The body unconditionally serializes `qty` (str(order.get('qty')) -> 'None' when a notional-only order is passed) and hard-codes time_in_force='day'. Alpaca supports notional (fractional dollar) orders that send `notional` instead of `qty`, and limit orders frequently need gtc/ioc TIF. As written, a notional order sends qty='None' and is rejected, and the order_ttl_cycles/limit semantics elsewhere in the config cannot be honored.
fix: Send `qty` only when present, else `notional`; map TIF from the order (`order.get('time_in_force')`) defaulting to 'day'. Omit qty key when order has no qty.

title: positions() assumes a list; an Alpaca error envelope (dict) crashes the comprehension
description: `positions()` does `data = self._request(...) or []` then `[... for p in data]`. If Alpaca returns a JSON object (e.g. an error/message dict) with HTTP 200, `data` is a truthy dict and the comprehension iterates keys, making `p.get(...)` a str.get → AttributeError. Reconciliation against broker truth then crashes.
fix: Coerce to list: `data = self._request('GET','/v2/positions'); data = data if isinstance(data, list) else []`.

title: AlpacaBroker.__init__ leases keys and asserts gates at construction; any later config change (live toggle) is not reflected
description: mode/base/keys are bound once in __init__ from config. If live_trading_enabled is toggled on after the object is constructed, this instance keeps the paper base/keys; conversely a cached live instance keeps hitting LIVE_BASE after the operator flips live off, since _assert_enabled isn't re-checked per request. A long-lived broker instance can thus route orders to the wrong (live) endpoint relative to current config.
fix: Re-read live flag and re-assert gating per submit() (or don't cache the broker across config changes); at least re-check live_trading_enabled before each live submit.

title: Kelly factor cannot fall below 1.0 even with negative edge
description: After computing the Kelly bet fraction, the return is _clamp(bet/0.20, 0.25, 2.5). When kelly is <=0 (losing system: p - (1-p)/b < 0), bet is clamped to 0.0 at line 252, so bet/0.20 = 0.0, then clamped up to the 0.25 floor — meaning a system with zero/negative edge still sizes at 0.25x rather than being vetoed. More importantly the floor 0.25 means Kelly never returns a sub-0.25 reduction, so a genuinely bad edge is never throttled below quarter-size. The intent ('fractional Kelly') implies smaller-or-zero sizing for poor edge.
fix: Lower the floor (e.g. _clamp(bet/0.20, 0.0, 2.5)) so a non-positive Kelly can shrink size toward zero, or special-case kelly<=0 to return a small/zero factor; keep the 0.20 neutral reference.

title: _ann_vol/_atr period mismatch can silently disable vol sizing
description: _vol_target_factor calls _ann_vol(_closes(symbol,'6mo')). portfolio_insights.annualized_vol needs sufficient closes; with a short 6mo window or holidays it may return None, falling back to 1.0 (no vol targeting) without any signal. Not itself a crash, but combined with _atr requiring len(bars) < period+1 → None, vol-target and ATR-stop enhancements quietly no-op on thinly-traded or newly-listed symbols. Worth flagging as a correctness/coverage gap.
fix: Use a longer window (e.g. '1y') for _ann_vol/_atr inputs, or log.debug when the factor falls back so silent no-ops are observable.

title: Relative-strength gate recomputes SPY closes with wrong period semantics vs symbol
description: In gate 8 the symbol's _pct_return uses `closes` cached as _closes(symbol,'1y') but the market series is _pct_return(_market_closes('1y'), lb). That is consistent. However at line 410 (gate 9) `closes` may already have been populated from the '1y' fetch in gate 6/7/8 and is then reused for correlation which the comment says wants '6mo'. The cached `closes` (1y) is passed to _returns for correlation while peers use _returns(_closes(s,'6mo')) (6mo) — mismatched lengths are truncated by _correlation's min(len) but the symbol's 1y series biases the correlation window/series alignment vs peers.
fix: For the correlation gate, fetch the symbol's 6mo series explicitly (e.g. sym_ret_series = _returns(_closes(symbol,'6mo'))) instead of reusing the possibly-1y cached `closes`.

title: closes cache fetched with 1y is reused where 6mo is intended (and vice versa)
description: The `closes` local is lazily set on first use. If gate 6/7/8 (which fetch '1y') run first, the same `closes` is reused by gate 9's correlation block (line 410 `closes if closes is not None else _closes(symbol,'6mo')`), so the '6mo' branch never executes once any 1y branch has run. Conversely if only gate 9 runs first it caches '6mo' and gates 6/7/8 would reuse the shorter series. Period selection is therefore order-dependent and frequently wrong.
fix: Use separate locals for the two windows (e.g. closes_1y and closes_6mo) each lazily fetched with its own period, instead of one shared `closes`.

title: Profit-ratchet uses live peak_mark that is never reset after an exit
description: Gate 13 reads peak_mark from aj_position_state. update_position_state (aj_rules) only ever raises peak via max() and sets it NULL on going flat. If a position is partially reduced then re-added, peak_mark persists from the prior high, so peak_gain stays inflated and the ratchet can fire immediately on re-entry (peak_gain>=ratchet while current gain<=lock). This produces spurious immediate exits on re-entered names.
fix: On a buy that opens/re-opens a position (held was 0), reset peak_mark to the current mark in update_position_state, or key the ratchet off a peak recorded since the most recent open rather than the persisted all-time peak.

title: recent_hit_rate ignores the requested n when fewer than 5 of the LAST n exist but more total
description: recent_hit_rate does _realized_trades()[-n:] then requires len>=5. If there are e.g. 4 total trades it returns None (fine). But the slice [-n:] caps the sample at n; that's intended. The subtle bug: realized_trades is ordered by filled_at ASC, so [-n:] is the most recent n — correct. No defect here on reflection; however recent_hit_rate counts 'realized>0' as a win but treats realized==0 (scratch) as a loss in the denominator, biasing the hit-rate downward and feeding adaptive_thresholds. Document/handle scratch trades.
fix: Exclude exact-zero realized trades from the denominator, or count them separately, so scratch trades don't depress the adaptive hit-rate that tightens thresholds.

title: rank_universe sorts by -score but ties/None scores collapse silently to 0.0
description: _radar_score returns 0.0 on any exception or short history, so symbols with no data are indistinguishable from genuine 0-score setups and can crowd into the top-K ahead of slightly-negative but valid setups. Sorting key=lambda t:-t[1] also makes NaN scores (if pi.momentum_score returns NaN) sort unpredictably. Top-K candidate selection can therefore surface data-less symbols.
fix: Have _radar_score return a sentinel (e.g. None or float('-inf')) for no-data symbols and filter/sink them before taking top-K; guard against NaN with math.isnan.

title: _earnings_days_away floor-divides total_seconds() producing wrong day count for past/negative
description: return int((dt - utc_now()).total_seconds() // 86400). Integer floor-division of a negative total_seconds (earnings already passed) rounds toward negative infinity, e.g. -0.5 days → -1, and the caller's blackout check `0 <= d <= eb` then behaves on a skewed value. Also for a date later today (0.4 days) // gives 0 (fine) but 23h59m before earnings gives 0 too — boundary days are mislabeled, affecting the earnings blackout gate.
fix: Use round() or compute calendar-day difference on the date components (dt.date() - now.date()).days rather than floor-dividing seconds.

title: Unrealized P&L rounds each position with money() then sums, accumulating rounding bias
description: attribution() computes unreal = aj_db.money((mark-avg)*qty) per symbol then d['total']=money(realized+unreal). positions_detail likewise sums already-rounded r['unrealized']. Rounding each leg to cents before summing introduces up to half-a-cent bias per position in totals; for many positions the aggregate can drift versus a single rounding at the end. For a trading P&L view this misstates totals.
fix: Carry full-precision intermediate values and apply money() only at the final aggregation (sum raw unrealized, then money() the total), or document that per-line cents rounding is intentional.

title: journal_csv notional uses round() not aj_db.money(), inconsistent rounding mode
description: notional = round(float(qty)*float(price),2) uses Python banker's rounding (ROUND_HALF_EVEN), whereas the rest of the system uses aj_db.money (ROUND_HALF_UP). The exported journal's notional column can differ by a cent from the same figure computed elsewhere, breaking reconciliation against P&L derived via money().
fix: notional = aj_db.money(float(r.get('qty') or 0) * float(r.get('price') or 0)) for consistency.

title: sharpe_like sample variance divides by (n-1) but guards len>=3, fine; but zero-PnL days inflate denominator
description: sharpe_like uses every equity_curve point's day_pnl_usd including days with 0 P&L (no trades). Idle days with day_pnl=0 shrink the mean and the stdev unpredictably, distorting the annualized Sharpe (multiplying by sqrt(252) assumes daily trading-day cadence, but equity_curve has one point per calendar date present, possibly with gaps). The sqrt(252) annualization is therefore inconsistent with the actual sampling frequency.
fix: Either annualize using the actual number of distinct trading days represented, or document that 0-PnL/idle days are intentionally included; at minimum skip weekend/holiday gaps when annualizing.

title: notify_fill builds AppleScript by string-formatting unsanitized symbol/side into osascript
description: display notification "{}" interpolates msg, which contains symbol and side.
