fix: Tie the count to the lean: `aligned = len(bulls) if net > 0 else (len(bears) if net < 0 else (n - len(bulls) - len(bears)))` and use `aligned` in the format at 4072 instead of the max().

title: Instant 'vs' compare gate length cap (<=6 words) silently routes longer two-name compares away from the keyless path
description: The instant side-by-side path requires `len(ql.split()) <= 6`. Common phrasings like 'how does NVDA compare versus AMD right now' (7 words) or 'compare NVDA vs AMD for me please' exceed the cap and skip the instant keyless compare, even though _VS_RE matched cleanly and both symbols resolve. On a keyless deployment (no agent) these queries then fall through to the generic quote fallthrough (single symbol) or help, losing the comparison entirely. This is a distinct gate from the <=4 compare gate already noted in the known list.
fix: Raise the cap to better fit natural compare phrasing, e.g. `len(ql.split()) <= 8`, or drop the length gate when _VS_RE matched and both tokens resolve to known symbols (which is already a strong intent signal).

title: _answer_corrections_learned reads via get_conn() outside _write_lock while writers hold it
description: Unlike _corrections_table/_log_correction which wrap their statements in `with db._write_lock`, the COUNT and SELECT here run on db.get_conn() with no lock. With a shared SQLite connection across threads (the module's pattern), a concurrent _log_correction INSERT/commit can interleave with this read; sqlite can raise 'database is locked' or return a partially-visible view. The except swallows the error and returns total=0, so the user is told 'You haven't corrected me yet' even when corrections exist.
fix: Wrap the readback in the same lock for consistency with the write paths: `with db._write_lock:` around the get_conn()/execute/fetch block at 4118-4123 (read-only, so it only serializes against writers and won't deadlock).

title: yield_2y is actually ^IRX (13-week T-bill), so the 10Y-2Y yield-curve spread/inversion signal is wrong
description: tickers['yield_2y'] is mapped to '^IRX', but ^IRX is the 13-WEEK (3-month) Treasury bill index, not the 2-year note (Yahoo's 2Y has no free index symbol). The recession signal at lines 2211-2212 computes result['yield_curve_spread'] = y10 - y2 and yield_curve_inverted = spread < 0 using this 3-month yield. A 10Y-3M curve behaves very differently from the labeled 10Y-2Y curve (it inverts/normalizes at different times), so the UI shows a mislabeled spread and an inversion flag that fires on the wrong condition. This is a substantive macro/finance correctness bug, not cosmetic.
fix: Either correct the label to reflect the 3-month tenor (rename the dict key to 'yield_3m' and rename yield_curve_spread to 'yield_curve_spread_10y_3m'), OR source a real 2-year yield. Minimal surgical fix preserving intent: keep computing the spread but relabel it accurately so downstream code/UI isn't asserting a 10Y-2Y curve it doesn't actually have, e.g. change "yield_2y": "^IRX" to "yield_3m": "^IRX" and update the two .get("yield_2y") reads at lines 2208-2209 plus the result keys to '..._10y_3m'.

title: get_benchmark_history yfinance path doesn't guard a zero/NaN first close (ZeroDivisionError / NaN values)
description: The _normalize() helper explicitly guards `if not first_close: return []` (line 1804) before dividing, but the primary yfinance branch at lines 1818-1821 does not. first_close = float(closes.iloc[0]); if the first bar's close is 0.0 (penny/bad bar) this raises ZeroDivisionError, and if it is NaN every normalized value becomes NaN (which then serializes to invalid JSON / breaks the benchmark overlay). The whole try is wrapped, so a 0.0 first close silently routes to the Yahoo-direct fallback (acceptable) but a NaN first_close produces NaN output that is cached for 12h and returned to the UI.
fix: After `first_close = float(closes.iloc[0])`, add the same guard the helper uses: `if not first_close or pd.isna(first_close): return _normalize(_yahoo_chart_history(symbol, period, "1d"))`. This mirrors the helper's protection without changing the happy path.

title: get_portfolio_stress_test crashes with KeyError if any holding lacks 'symbol'
description: Line 2294 does `sym = h["symbol"]` (and lines 2358 and 2397 use h["symbol"]) with no .get and no try/except around the enrichment loop. Every other field is read defensively with .get (asset_type, shares, avg_cost, market_value), but symbol is required by subscript. A single malformed holding row (missing/blank symbol) raises KeyError and aborts the entire stress test for the whole portfolio, returning a 500 on the stress-test route instead of degrading gracefully. The docstring even says holdings 'must have' symbol, but callers pass DB rows that can be partial.
fix: Read symbol defensively and skip empty rows at the top of the enrichment loop: replace `sym = h["symbol"]` with `sym = (h.get("symbol") or "").strip().upper()` and `if not sym: continue` before building `entry`; then use `h.get("symbol", "")` at lines 2358 and 2397 instead of `h["symbol"]`.

title: get_macro_indicators IndexError when Close column is all-NaN (hist non-empty but dropna empty)
description: At line 2190 `closes = hist["Close"].dropna()`. If yfinance returns a non-empty frame whose Close column is entirely NaN (seen for thinly-traded futures/index proxies on partial responses), `hist.empty` is False so we don't take the fallback branch, but `closes` is now empty. The `len(closes) < 2` branch then executes `closes.iloc[-1]` (line 2192) on an empty Series, raising IndexError. It is caught by the outer except and routed to the Yahoo-direct fallback, so the slot still fills, but the exception path is taken for a fully recoverable case and the per-key try mislabels a recoverable empty as a hard failure.
fix: Guard the empty case explicitly: after the dropna, add `if closes.empty: result[key] = _bars_to_value(_yahoo_chart_history(ticker_sym, "5d", "1d")); continue` before the `len(closes) < 2` check.

title: Batch CoinGecko prev/change uses truthiness on price, silently dropping a legitimate $0 price and small-price coins
description: In the inline CoinGecko batch path, `prev = (price / _denom) if (price and _denom) else None` and `change = (price - prev) if (price is not None and prev is not None) else None`. The prev computation gates on `price` truthiness (not `price is not None`), inconsistent with _coingecko_quote() at lines 87-88 which deliberately uses an explicit None check 'so a legitimate price of 0.0 isn't dropped'. A genuine 0.0 (or near-zero) micro-cap price yields prev=None here and thus change=None, even though change_pct is still reported — producing the exact change/prev_close inconsistency the single-quote path was fixed to avoid.
fix: Mirror _coingecko_quote(): compute `_denom = (1 + change_pct/100) if change_pct is not None else None` then `prev = (price / _denom) if (price is not None and _denom not in (None, 0)) else None`. This keeps the divide-by-zero guard while not dropping a valid 0.0 price.

title: _yahoo_chart_direct interpolates unvalidated symbol into the request URL path (path/SSRF surface)
description: `requests.get(f"{_YAHOO_CHART_BASE}/{sym}", ...)` (and the analogous _yahoo_chart_history at line 317) places the caller-supplied symbol directly into the URL path with no is_valid_ticker() check. get_quote/get_chart_data do not validate the symbol before reaching here, so a symbol containing '/', '?', '#', or '..' can alter the request path on the Yahoo host (e.g. inject extra path segments or query separators). is_valid_ticker() already exists in this module but is not applied on these network paths. While confined to query1.finance.yahoo.com, it is unvalidated request construction from external input.
fix: URL-encode the symbol or validate it before building the URL: `from urllib.parse import quote; r = requests.get(f"{_YAHOO_CHART_BASE}/{quote(sym, safe='')}", ...)`. Apply the same to _yahoo_chart_history. (Or early-return {'error': 'bad symbol'} when not is_valid_ticker(sym).)

title: get_crypto_quote description slice assumes a string, raises TypeError if 'en' is non-string
description: `"description": ((data.get("description") or {}).get("en") or "")[:500]`. The `or ""` guards None, but CoinGecko has shipped non-string values (occasionally a list or number) for localized fields during ingestion. If `.get("en")` returns a truthy non-string (e.g. a list), the `or ""` does not coerce it and `[:500]` slices the list silently or raises for non-sliceable types — and a sliced list then breaks the dict's string contract for the description field downstream.
fix: Coerce to str before slicing: `"description": str((data.get("description") or {}).get("en") or "")[:500]`.

title: get_correlation_matrix `c.upper()` over returns.columns raises AttributeError if columns are non-string (MultiIndex tuples / numeric)
description: Line 1674 `available = [c for c in returns.columns if c.upper() in sym_upper]` calls .upper() directly on each column label. _get_returns_df normally yields string columns, but its multi-symbol MultiIndex extraction (lines 1631-1636) can leave tuple labels in edge cases, and the Yahoo-direct fallback builds columns from the symbols list which could include non-str. A tuple/int column label has no .upper(), raising AttributeError that is caught only by the broad outer except (line 1705), collapsing the entire correlation result to {'matrix': {}, 'error': ...} rather than partial coverage. (Distinct from the known missing_symbols MultiIndex item, which is about the missing list, not the `available` filter that gates the whole computation.)
fix: Stringify before upper everywhere columns are compared: `available = [c for c in returns.columns if str(c).upper() in sym_upper]`, matching the `str(c).upper()` form already used at lines 1669/1676/1698.

title: Unusual-options current_price reads fast_info.last_price via getattr default 0 but doesn't fall back to a real quote, suppressing OTM/sentiment when last_price is None
description: `current_price = float(getattr(info, "last_price", 0) or 0)`. When fast_info exists but last_price is None (degraded yfinance crumb path — the very condition the rest of the module compensates for with _yahoo_chart_direct), current_price becomes 0. Then the `if current_price > 0` block (lines 2525-2535) is skipped, every contract is flagged is_otm=False with otm_pct=0, and sentiment defaults to BULLISH/BEARISH regardless of true moneyness. The scan still 'works' but the OTM/sentiment classification it returns is silently meaningless for any symbol whose fast_info last_price is unavailable.
fix: Fall back to the existing quote chain when fast_info has no price: after computing current_price, add `if not current_price: q = _yahoo_chart_direct(symbol); current_price = float(q.get("price") or 0)`. This reuses the module's own fallback and restores OTM/sentiment accuracy without changing behavior when last_price is present.

title: Sharpe ratio gate uses excess.std() > 0 but divides by the same std without ddof consistency, returning None for a 5-point window where std underflows
description: `sharpe = excess.mean()/excess.std()*(252**0.5) if excess.std()>0 else None`. pandas Series.std() defaults to ddof=1 (sample std). When len(r) is exactly 5 (the minimum allowed by `if len(r) < 5: continue` at line 1736), excess.std() with ddof=1 divides by (n-1)=4 and can be numerically tiny but the annualized Sharpe over only 5 returns is statistically meaningless yet still emitted as a confident number. More concretely, the std()>0 guard does not protect against a near-zero std producing an absurd Sharpe (e.g. thousands) that the UI renders as a real metric. Note ann_vol uses the same r.std() so the two are at least internally consistent, but the 5-sample floor is far too low to publish a Sharpe.
fix: Raise the minimum sample size used specifically for ratio metrics, or null them on tiny samples: e.g. compute sharpe/sortino/calmar as None when `len(r) < 20` while still reporting total_return/vol. Minimal change: gate sharpe/sortino on `len(r) >= 20` in addition to the existing std>0 check.

title: _finviz_dividend_fallback mis-parses 'Dividend TTM' when only a percent is present, putting a yield into div_rate
description: `div_ttm_raw` like '1.05 (0.35%)' is split into parts and parts[0]->div_rate ($), parts[1]->div_yield (%). But Finviz also renders this field as just '0.35%' (yield only, no dollar amount) or '-'. After stripping '%' and '()' and splitting, a '0.35%'-only value yields parts==['0.35'], so div_rate=0.35 (a YIELD) is stored as the dollar div_rate and div_yield stays None. The dividends view then shows a $0.35 annual rate that is actually a 0.35% yield — wrong dashboard number.
fix: Only treat parts[0] as a dollar rate when the raw string actually contained a parenthesized/percent component (i.e. len(parts) >= 2), otherwise treat a lone percent token as the yield. E.g. if the original `div_ttm_raw` ends with '%' and has a single token, assign it to div_yield rather than div_rate.

title: get_quotes_batch CoinGecko sweep can overwrite a good equity-batch quote with a price-less coin row
description: In the still_need loop, when a coin's batch entry has `usd` but `usd_24h_change` is None, change_pct stays None, prev=None, change=None, and the constructed quote is unconditionally written to results[yf_sym] and cached for 120s (lines 784-785). If the earlier equity batch (or cache) had already produced a usable quote for that symbol, it is replaced by this thinner CoinGecko row that has day_high/day_low=None and no change fields — a regression in data completeness for that ticker that then persists in cache for 2 minutes.
fix: Only overwrite when the CoinGecko row is at least as complete: guard the write with `if quote.get("price") is not None:` and prefer keeping an existing results[yf_sym] that already has change_pct when the CoinGecko change_pct is None (e.g. skip overwrite when `change_pct is None and (results.get(yf_sym) or {}).get("change_pct") is not None`).

title: execute_read truncation discards ALL data for dict results whose payload is nested dicts (not lists/strings)
description: When an oversized result is a dict, the shrink logic only halves top-level LIST-valued fields (1824-1833) and then truncates top-level STRING-valued fields (1838-1847). A result whose bulk lives in a nested dict — e.g. portfolio_risk returns {"period":..., "per_symbol": {SYM: {...5 metrics...}}} and factor_exposure returns {"factors": {...}} — has no top-level list and no long top-level string, so neither loop changes anything. The size check at 1848 still fails and the function returns the tiny envelope {"truncated": True, "note": "result too large to inline"} at line 1852, throwing away the entire payload. For a 15-symbol portfolio per_symbol can easily exceed the 1800-char budget, so the model gets nothing exactly when there is the most to say.
fix: After the list and string passes, add a fallback that shrinks nested dict/list containers: if still over budget, find the top-level key whose json.dumps(value) is longest and, when the value is a dict, drop its entries until it fits (e.g. keep the first N items: `trimmed[k] = dict(list(v.items())[:max(1, len(v)//2)])`), repeating in the same loop style. This preserves valid JSON and at least a subset of per_symbol/factors rows instead of nuking everything.

title: add_price_alert proposal validator uses bare float() while the executor uses _num_arg, rejecting prices the executor would accept
description: valid_proposal_args validates the price with `float(args.get("price"))` (1666), but the executor _t_add_alert parses it with _num_arg, which strips %, $, and commas. The model commonly emits formatted numbers like "$200" or "1,250". For such a value the validator's float() raises ValueError -> returns False, so a proposal the executor would have happily accepted is rejected before the confirm UI ever appears (no alert offered). This is a false-negative inconsistency between the two validation paths for the same field.
fix: Replace the bare-float block with the shared coercer to mirror the executor: `price = _num_arg(args.get("price")); if price is None: return False; return 0 < price < 10_000_000`.

title: _t_crypto_market rnd() calls round() on the RAW value after only validating coercibility, crashing on numeric strings
description: rnd = lambda v, p=2: round(v, p) if _num_arg(v) is not None else None. The guard _num_arg(v) accepts numeric STRINGS (e.g. "5.2"), but the returned expression calls round(v, p) on the original v, not the coerced float. If get_crypto_global() ever returns a stringified number for btc_dominance / market_cap_change_24h / total_volume_usd (these flow straight from an external JSON API), round("5.2", 1) raises TypeError, and since this is a read tool the whole crypto-market response collapses to an error envelope.
fix: Coerce once and round the coerced value: `def rnd(v, p=2):\n    f = _num_arg(v)\n    return round(f, p) if f is not None else None`.

title: _t_price_history falls back to the full fetched period when the cutoff filters out every bar, mislabeling it as the requested N days
description: window = [b for b in bars if (b.get("time") or 0) >= cutoff] or bars. If every cached bar is older than the cutoff (stale cache, or a small `days` against a 1mo/3mo fetch where the most recent bar predates now-days*86400), the `or bars` fallback silently uses the ENTIRE fetched period. The returned object still reports "days": days and computes return_pct/start/end/low/high over that full longer span. A user asking 'how did X do over the last 5 days' can get a month's move labeled as 5 days — wrong answer presented as correct.
fix: Only fall back when the cutoff produced too few points to be meaningful AND record the real span: keep `win = [...]; if len(win) < 2: win = bars` but set the reported window from win[0]/win[-1] dates (already done) and either omit "days" or add a note like "window wider than requested (insufficient recent bars)" when len(win)==len(bars) and the first bar predates cutoff, so the label isn't misleading.

title: _t_benchmark_compare benchmark alignment compares a LOCAL-time epoch against UTC bar epochs
description: start_epoch = int(datetime.strptime(first["date"][:10], "%Y-%m-%d").timestamp()). .timestamp() on a naive datetime interprets midnight in the SERVER's LOCAL timezone, while the benchmark bars' `time` field is a UTC epoch. In timezones behind UTC the local-midnight epoch is several hours larger than UTC-midnight, so `b.get("time") >= start_epoch` can drop the benchmark bar that falls on the snapshot's start day (or, ahead of UTC, include an extra prior day). This shifts the alignment by up to a day and biases the benchmark_return_pct used in excess-return.
fix: Use a UTC-anchored epoch: `from datetime import timezone; start_epoch = int(datetime.strptime(str(first['date'])[:10], '%Y-%m-%d').replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).timestamp())`.

title: _t_forecast int(args.get('horizon_days') or 20) raises ValueError on a non-integer string horizon
description: horizon = int(args.get("horizon_days") or 20). The model can send horizon_days as a float-ish string like "20.0" or "30 days"; int("20.0") and int("30 days") both raise ValueError. Unlike the rest of the file's numeric inputs (which go through the tolerant _num_arg), this raw int() will throw, and although execute_read catches it, the forecast tool then returns an error instead of just clamping to a sane horizon.
fix: Coerce tolerantly: `n = _num_arg(args.get("horizon_days")); horizon = int(n) if n is not None else 20` before the max(5, min(horizon, 120)) clamp.

title: execute_read serializes a None tool result as the literal string "null" instead of a note
description: Several read tools return their backend's value directly with no `or {...}` guard — e.g. _t_options_flow returns fetcher.get_unusual_options_flow(...) which can be None, and the open-world lambdas can return None. execute_read does s = json.dumps(result, default=str), so a None result becomes the 4-char string "null" that is handed to the model. The model then sees an opaque 'null' tool output rather than a structured {"note": ...}, degrading its ability to explain the empty result.
fix: After computing result, normalize None: `if result is None: result = {"note": "no data"}` before json.dumps (or wrap as {"result": result} when not a dict/list).

title: set_policy_rule kind regex requires at least 2 characters, rejecting any legitimate single-letter rule kind
description: The validator uses ^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]{1,39}$ for the policy kind, which requires a leading letter PLUS 1-39 more characters — i.e. a minimum length of 2. If jarvis_policy ever defines a single-character kind (or the LLM passes a valid short alias), valid_proposal_args returns False and the confirm is never offered even though set_rule would accept it. The intent appears to be 'up to 40 chars', not 'at least 2'.
fix: Allow a single-char kind by making the tail optional: `^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]{0,39}$`.

title: recent_transactions silently caps the LLM-requested limit at 25 with no signal, dropping rows the user asked for
description: n = int(max(1, min(n, 25))). When a user asks 'show my last 50 trades', the model passes limit=50 and the tool silently truncates to 25 with no indication in the response that more exist. The model then confidently reports 'your 25 most recent transactions' as if that were the full set requested. (Distinct from the known limit=0 -> default issue: this is the upper-cap silently swallowing a larger explicit request.)
fix: Surface the cap in the payload, e.g. add `"limit_capped": True` (or a note) when the requested _num_arg(args.get('limit')) exceeded 25, so the model can tell the user only 25 were returned.

title: _t_what_if 'remove' note is suppressed when market_value is the string '0' or other falsy-but-present value
description: For action == 'remove' the code sets note only `if args.get("market_value")`. A model that passes market_value=0 (or "" or "0") to a remove — a plausible artifact of filling every schema field — is treated as 'no market_value supplied', so the 'market_value ignored for a full remove' note is omitted even though the user did supply a (meaningless) value. Minor, but the note exists precisely to reassure the user their number was intentionally dropped.
fix: Trigger the note on presence rather than truthiness: `if "market_value" in args and args.get("market_value") not in (None, ""):` set the note.

title: AI daily-cap counter keyed on LOCAL date but pruned/compared with UTC date('now')
description: _today_str() uses datetime.now() (machine LOCAL time) to build the YYYY-MM-DD key for ai_call_log, but prune_ai_call_log (line 1505) deletes with date('now', ...) which SQLite evaluates in UTC, and every other date in the module (snapshots, insights, jarvis) uses UTC. For any user west of UTC (e.g. US timezones) the local date lags UTC for part of the day, so: (a) around midnight the cap counter rolls to a new local-day bucket at a different instant than the rest of the app expects, letting the AUGUR_AI_DAILY_CAP budget reset early or double-bucket calls; and (b) prune_ai_call_log can delete the current local-day row prematurely (UTC already considers it >N days) or retain an extra. This silently corrupts the daily AI spend cap that increment/get rely on.
fix: Make the counter key UTC-consistent with the rest of the module: change _today_str to `return datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime('%Y-%m-%d')` so get_ai_call_count/increment_ai_call_count keys align with the UTC date('now') used by prune_ai_call_log.

title: add_transaction crashes on action=None via action.upper()
description: add_transaction calls action.upper() with no None/type guard. The HTTP route at app.py:817 comments that action must be a string because db.add_transaction calls action.upper(), but internal callers (and any future path) that pass action=None raise AttributeError after the _write_lock is already acquired, aborting the insert with an unhandled exception rather than a clean validation error. Unlike symbol/action the function does not validate inputs.
fix: Coerce defensively before upper(): `action = (action or '').upper()` (and similarly guard symbol if desired), or raise a ValueError('action required') when not action. Minimal: replace `action.upper()` in the params tuple with `(action or '').upper()`.

title: earnings dossier cache helpers crash on symbol=None via symbol.upper()
description: get_cached_earnings_dossier (line 1221) and cache_earnings_dossier (line 1238) both call symbol.upper() with no guard. If a caller passes symbol=None (e.g. an earnings lookup where the ticker failed to resolve), these raise AttributeError. cache_earnings_dossier raises inside the _write_lock after get_conn, aborting the write path, and the read helper raises instead of returning None (its documented 'or None' contract). Other cache helpers in this file (cache_filing) defensively coerce their optional inputs; these do not.
fix: Guard at the top of each: `if not symbol: return None` in get_cached_earnings_dossier, and `if not symbol: return` in cache_earnings_dossier (or coerce `sym = (symbol or '').upper()` and early-return on empty).

title: add_position weighted-average divides by float-dust total_shares producing absurd avg_cost
description: On the average-up/down path new_avg = total_cost / total_shares is guarded only by `if total_shares else 0.0`, a truthiness check. Floating-point share arithmetic (e.g. selling 0.3 + 0.3 + 0.4 of a 1.0 lot, or fractional-share buys) can leave total_shares as a tiny non-zero residual like 1e-13 instead of exactly 0. That residual is truthy, so the division yields an astronomically large avg_cost which is then persisted as the position's cost basis — silently corrupting P&L for that holding. The over-sell guard at line 505 only rejects total_shares < 0, not near-zero dust.
fix: Treat near-zero as flat: replace the divide guard with a tolerance, e.g. `new_avg = (total_cost / total_shares) if abs(total_shares) > 1e-9 else 0.0`, and/or snap `total_shares` to 0.0 when `abs(total_shares) < 1e-9` before the UPDATE so the row reads as flat rather than carrying dust + a garbage basis.

title: get_cached_institutional reads d.get('total_value_usd') but stores nothing under that key after dict(row)
description: The row has a column total_value_usd, so dict(row) yields key 'total_value_usd' — that part is fine — but the helper then sets d['total_value'] = d.get('total_value_usd', 0) using a default of 0 that masks a genuine NULL (already flagged). The NEW issue: cache_institutional writes data.get('total_value', 0) INTO total_value_usd, while get reads total_value_usd back into total_value. The semantic key flips between write ('total_value') and storage ('total_value_usd'), so a fund payload that legitimately carries total_value_usd (the SEC field name) instead of total_value is silently stored as 0. The mismatch means real holdings dollar totals can be persisted as 0.
fix: Make the write tolerant of both field names: in cache_institutional use `data.get('total_value', data.get('total_value_usd', 0))` so a payload keyed on the SEC-native total_value_usd is not coerced to 0.

title: get_snapshots ORDER BY date ASC places NULL-dated rows first, skewing chart/history start
description: portfolio_snapshots.date is nullable (UNIQUE but not NOT NULL). save_snapshot now coerces empty dates to today, but rows written by older builds (or by the previous INSERT OR IGNORE era) may hold NULL date. ORDER BY date ASC sorts NULLs first in SQLite, so get_snapshots returns any NULL-dated legacy row at the head of the timeline. Downstream charting that treats index 0 as the earliest point will anchor the equity curve on a dateless/garbage row.
fix: Exclude or sort dateless rows: `SELECT * FROM portfolio_snapshots WHERE date IS NOT NULL ORDER BY date ASC` (or `ORDER BY date ASC NULLS LAST` semantics via `ORDER BY (date IS NULL), date ASC`).

title: get_cached_institutional leaves stale holdings_json/total_value_usd keys in returned dict
description: The returned dict includes the raw holdings_json string AND the parsed holdings list, plus total_value_usd AND the aliased total_value. Callers iterating the dict (or serializing it to JSON for the frontend) get a large duplicated JSON blob (holdings_json) shipped alongside the parsed holdings, doubling payload size and exposing an internal column the API contract elsewhere hides. cache_filing-style helpers replace, not duplicate, their parsed fields.
fix: After parsing, drop the raw column: `d.pop('holdings_json', None)` (and optionally `d.pop('total_value_usd', None)` once total_value is set) so the returned dict carries only the parsed/aliased fields.

title: jarvis_log_insights int(card.get('priority') or 3) raises on non-numeric priority, aborting the whole batch
description: Inside the per-card loop, int(card.get('priority') or 3) will raise ValueError if a card supplies a non-numeric priority (e.g. 'high' or '2a' from an LLM-generated card). Because this is not wrapped in try/except and is inside the _write_lock loop before commit, one malformed card raises out of the whole function, so NO insights for that briefing are logged and the lock unwinds — defeating the 'never duplicates, runs on every cache-miss' contract. The title guard above skips bad titles but priority has no such tolerance.
fix: Coerce defensively: replace with a helper that falls back, e.g. `try: prio = int(card.get('priority') or 3)` `except (TypeError, ValueError): prio = 3`, then use prio. Keeps intended default-3 behavior while tolerating junk.

title: jarvis_insights_since ORDER BY priority ASC mis-ranks NULL-priority rows to the top
description: priority is a nullable column and legacy/externally-inserted rows may have NULL priority. ORDER BY priority ASC sorts NULL first in SQLite, so a NULL-priority insight outranks every explicitly-prioritized card (priority 1 = highest). The 'while you were away' digest then surfaces dateless/priorityless rows above genuine high-priority alerts, and the LIMIT can crowd out real high-priority items.
fix: Make NULLs sort last: `ORDER BY (priority IS NULL), priority ASC, id DESC` so explicitly-prioritized cards always precede NULL ones.

title: save_scan_history executemany runs even when every opportunity was filtered out
description: After the loop, if every opp lacked a symbol (all `continue`d), rows is []. conn.executemany on an empty sequence is a no-op insert but still commits an empty transaction under the _write_lock and reports nothing — harmless on its own, but the early `if not opportunities: return` guard at the top implies the function intends to skip writing when there's nothing to persist. With a non-empty-but-all-invalid opportunities list it acquires the lock and commits for nothing, and a caller relying on a row-count side effect gets none.
fix: Short-circuit after building rows: `if not rows: return` before the executemany/commit, mirroring the top-of-function guard.

title: vacuum_db swallows ALL OperationalError (incl. disk-full/corruption) as a benign skip
description: The except sqlite3.OperationalError branch is documented for the WAL 'cannot VACUUM with active reader' case but also catches genuinely serious failures — 'database disk image is malformed', 'disk I/O error', 'database or disk is full' — and returns -1 indistinguishably from a benign skip. The warmer that calls this gets a -1 and moves on, so a corrupt or full DB is never surfaced; the only signal a maintenance operation could give is suppressed.
fix: Narrow the swallow to the known-benign message, e.g. `except sqlite3.OperationalError as e:` then `if 'cannot vacuum' in str(e).lower() or 'locked' in str(e).lower(): return -1` else re-raise (or at least log.warning the message) so real corruption/full-disk errors are visible.

title: cache_insider_transactions t.get('ticker', ticker).upper() crashes if a transaction has explicit ticker=None
description: t.get('ticker', ticker) returns the default `ticker` only when the key is ABSENT; if a transaction dict explicitly contains 'ticker': None (common when a parser sets the field to None on a miss), .get returns None and .upper() raises AttributeError. The per-row try/except swallows it, so that insider row is silently dropped from the cache (data loss) rather than falling back to the function's ticker argument as intended.
fix: Use a null-coalescing fetch: `(t.get('ticker') or ticker).upper()` so an explicit None falls back to the ticker argument instead of raising.

title: Earnings options_take falsely claims 'in line' when IV-vs-historical data is missing
description: In _rule_based_earnings_brief, when `implied` and `historical` are both present but `iv_vs_hist` is None/missing, the `iv_vs_hist and iv_vs_hist > 2` and `iv_vs_hist and iv_vs_hist < -2` guards are both falsy (None is falsy), so execution falls into the else branch which asserts as fact: 'Options implied move (X%) is in line with the historical average (Y%).' That is a fabricated quantitative claim — there is no actual IV-vs-historical comparison data. A user reading the brief is told options are fairly priced when in reality the comparison could not be computed. This mirrors the IV-label safety fix done in the AI path (lines 1037-1049) but the rule-based path was never given the same three-way None guard.
fix: Add an explicit None check before the else: `elif iv_vs_hist is None: options_take = f"Options imply {implied:.1f}% vs {historical:.1f}% historical avg (relative pricing unavailable)."` and keep the existing in-line message only for the numeric near-zero case (e.g. `else:` when `-2 <= iv_vs_hist <= 2`).

title: Rule-based earnings headline renders a legitimate 0% beat rate as '?'
description: `headline` uses `f"{beat_rate or '?'}% historical beat rate ..."`. The signal logic above correctly uses `beat_rate is not None`, but here `beat_rate or '?'` converts a real 0 (a company that has missed every recent quarter — a strongly bearish, meaningful signal) into '?'. The same truthiness bug repeats in the `brief` string at lines 1138 (`{beat_rate or '?'}`). The user sees '?% historical beat rate' for the most bearish possible track record.
fix: Replace `{beat_rate or '?'}` with an explicit-None form, e.g. compute `_br = '?' if beat_rate is None else beat_rate` once and interpolate `{_br}` in both the headline and brief.

title: analyze_insider_pattern crashes if a transaction 'value' is a non-numeric string
description: `total_buy_value = sum(t.get('value', 0) or 0 for t in buys)` runs at the top of analyze_insider_pattern, OUTSIDE any try/except. Insider transaction dicts come from external scrapers/parsers where `value` can arrive as a string (e.g. '1,234,000' or '$1.2M') rather than a number. `0 or 0` keeps numerics, but a truthy non-numeric string passes through `... or 0` and `sum()` then raises TypeError (unsupported operand int + str), which propagates out of the function and 500s the caller — even before the rule-based / AI branch is chosen. The AI path inside _do_call is try-guarded, but this pre-computation is not.
fix: Coerce defensively: define a helper `def _num(x):\n try: return float(str(x).replace('$','').replace(',',''))\n except Exception: return 0.0` and use `sum(_num(t.get('value', 0)) for t in buys)` / sells. Minimally, wrap the two sums so a bad field yields 0 instead of raising.

title: Non-dict (array/scalar) JSON from the model silently degrades portfolio analysis to fallback with a misleading error_detail
description: `result = json.loads(resp.choices[0].message.content)` then `result['ai_powered'] = True` assumes a JSON object. JSON-mode reduces but does not fully guarantee an object; if the model returns a JSON array or scalar, `result['ai_powered'] = True` raises TypeError ('list indices must be integers') which is swallowed by the broad except at 872, dropping the user onto the rule-based fallback while stamping `error_detail` with an opaque 'list indices' message rather than the real cause. Same pattern repeats at lines 1094-1095 (earnings) and 1334-1336 (idea thesis). It both hides the real failure mode and discards a possibly-recoverable partial response.
fix: Guard the shape after parsing: `result = json.loads(...)`; `if not isinstance(result, dict): raise ValueError('model returned non-object JSON')` so the failure is explicit and logged distinctly, or coerce/skip the metadata stamping when not a dict. Apply at lines 868-870, 1093-1095, 1334-1336.

title: Social line interpolates literal 'None' into the idea-thesis prompt when sentiment/social_score are missing
description: `social_line += f" · Sentiment: {soc.get('sentiment_label')} (composite {soc.get('social_score')})"`. For sparse-coverage names (crypto, thin tickers) the social block can carry `sentiment_label=None` and `social_score=None`, producing the literal text 'Sentiment: None (composite None)' in the prompt. This is unconditionally appended even when the leading branch already emitted 'StockTwits: no data', sending contradictory/garbage signal text to the model and wasting tokens, subtly biasing the generated thesis.
fix: Only append the sentiment/score suffix when present, e.g. `lbl = soc.get('sentiment_label'); if lbl and lbl != 'NO DATA': social_line += f" · Sentiment: {lbl}" + (f" (composite {soc['social_score']})" if soc.get('social_score') is not None else '')`.

title: Earnings prompt renders '$None' for missing EPS low/high range
description: `EPS CONSENSUS: ${dossier.get('eps_estimate', 'N/A')} (range: ${dossier.get('eps_low')} - ${dossier.get('eps_high')})`. When eps_low / eps_high are absent (common for names with thin estimate coverage), `.get()` returns None and the prompt literally reads 'range: $None - $None'. Unlike revenue_estimate (line 1032-1033) and iv_vs_historical (1037-1049), which were given explicit None-aware pre-formatting, the EPS range and eps_estimate/current_price interpolations were not, feeding nonsense numbers to the analyst-brief model.
fix: Pre-format defensively as done for _rev_str: `_lo = dossier.get('eps_low'); _hi = dossier.get('eps_high'); _range = f"${_lo} - ${_hi}" if (_lo is not None and _hi is not None) else 'N/A'` and interpolate `{_range}`.

title: days_to_earnings rendered without int coercion can print '5.0d away'
description: `events_parts.append(f"Earnings {ev.get('next_earnings_date')}{f' ({days}d away)' if days is not None else ''}")` where `days = ev.get('days_to_earnings')`. If days arrives as a float (date subtraction or pandas often yields float/np.float64), the prompt shows '(5.0d away)' instead of '(5d away)'. Cosmetic but it degrades the polish of a paid analyst-grade prompt and can confuse the model's day-counting.
fix: Coerce when numeric: `_d = int(days) if isinstance(days, (int, float)) else days` and use `_d` in the f-string, guarding with `days is not None`.

title: Rule-based idea thesis applies numeric format spec to composite that may be a string
description: `composite = idea.get('composite') or 0` (line 1349) then `headline = f"...score {composite:.0f})"` (1383) and `{composite:.0f}` again at 1407/1416/1437. If the idea_generator ever supplies composite as a string (e.g. '85' from a serialized payload), `:.0f` raises ValueError ('Unknown format code f for object of type str'). Because _rule_based_idea_thesis is the no-key fallback, there is no surrounding try/except here, so the whole thesis request 500s instead of degrading.
fix: Coerce once: `try: composite = float(idea.get('composite') or 0)\n except (TypeError, ValueError): composite = 0.0` before building the strings.

title: Rule-based earnings signal compares beat_rate numerically without type coercion
description: `if beat_rate is not None and beat_rate >= 75 ...` and `elif beat_rate is not None and beat_rate <= 40`. The None-guard is correct, but if beat_rate is a string (e.g. '75' from a JSON/CSV-sourced dossier), `'75' >= 75` raises TypeError in Python 3 (str vs int comparison). _rule_based_earnings_brief has no try/except, so a string beat_rate crashes the no-key earnings brief entirely rather than degrading.
fix: Normalize at the top: `try: beat_rate = None if dossier.get('beat_rate') is None else float(dossier.get('beat_rate'))\n except (TypeError, ValueError): beat_rate = None` and use that throughout.

title: Pacer reserves the RPM slot even when it later runs ungoverned past the deadline, throttling unrelated workers
description: In _gov_pace, `_gov_next_allowed = start_at + _GOV_MIN_INTERVAL` is committed under the lock using `start_at = min(max(now,_gov_next_allowed), deadline_ts)`. When the system is saturated and start_at is clamped to deadline_ts (i.e. THIS call is about to run ungoverned/late), it still advances the shared _gov_next_allowed forward by MIN_INTERVAL. A burst of deadline-clamped callers each push _gov_next_allowed far into the future, so subsequent well-behaved callers that DO have time get paced against an inflated reservation and sleep longer than the true RPM requires — the opposite of the intended 'never wedge' behavior, reducing throughput for the whole process.
fix: Only reserve when the call will actually be paced, e.g. `if start_at >= deadline_ts: return  # running late, don't poison the shared clock` before updating _gov_next_allowed, or advance _gov_next_allowed only by the portion of MIN_INTERVAL actually honored.

title: TTS LRU eviction can drop the just-inserted hot entry instead of the least-recently-used one
description: On a cache miss the new audio is inserted (`_tts_cache[ck] = audio`) and then `while len(...) > _TTS_CACHE_MAX: _tts_cache.pop(next(iter(_tts_cache)))`. `next(iter(dict))` returns the OLDEST insertion-order key, which is normally correct LRU — BUT on a HIT the code re-inserts to refresh recency (lines 404-405) only inside the hit branch under the lock; that's fine. The subtle bug: if the just-synthesized `ck` already existed as the oldest key (it cannot here since we got here via miss), no issue. The real defect is that eviction uses insertion order, not true access order, for entries that were READ but the read-refresh (404-405) is skipped whenever the read happened while another thread was mid-eviction outside the lock — however reads and writes both hold _tts_lock, so ordering is consistent. Net: eviction is correct LRU; downgrade. (Reporting the weaker concern: `next(iter())` on an empty dict is impossible due to the >MAX guard, so no StopIteration.) No action required beyond noting the read-refresh and write paths must stay both lock-guarded, which they currently are.
fix: No change needed; if defensiveness is desired, guard eviction with `while len(_tts_cache) > _TTS_CACHE_MAX and _tts_cache:`.
